name: Commercial Airplane
visual_anchor: Sleek modern twin-engine wide-body jet airliner cruising above a sea of fluffy golden sunset clouds.
core_traits: Fixed-wing powered aircraft designed to transport passengers and cargo through the air
Powered by high-bypass turbofan jet engines mounted under swept wings
Pressurized passenger cabins cruise efficiently at 10,000 to 12,000 meters altitude
Originated from the Wright brothers' historic first controlled flight in 1903

facts_and_myths.claim: Commercial jetliner cabin air is completely recirculated stale air that breeds disease.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Airliner air is refreshed every 2-3 minutes with outside air filtered through hospital-grade HEPA filters capturing 99.97% of microbes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Cabin air is often cleaner than the air in standard office buildings.

facts_and_myths.claim: Airplane toilets flush waste out of the bottom of the plane into mid-air during flight.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Toilets use high-velocity vacuum suction into sealed holding tanks, emptied on the ground by ground service trucks.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Vacuum toilets were patented by James Kemper in 1975.

name: Steam Locomotive
visual_anchor: Mighty black iron steam locomotive billowing white steam and glowing firebox embers as it thunders across a brick viaduct.
core_traits: Railway vehicle that produces power through a steam engine burning coal or wood
Powered the Industrial Revolution across Britain, Europe, and the American frontier
Features a horizontal fire-tube boiler, piston driving rods, and an iconic steam whistle
Gradually replaced in the 20th century by diesel-electric and electric trains

facts_and_myths.claim: Steam locomotives had to continuously shovel coal by hand in all operations.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Firemen manually shoveled tons of coal per trip into glowing fireboxes before mechanical stokers were invented.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Mallard locomotive holds the world speed record for steam trains at 202.6 km/h (126 mph).

facts_and_myths.claim: Early doctors warned that human bodies would disintegrate if trains traveled over 30 mph.
facts_and_myths.explanation: During the 1830s, critics and doctors genuinely feared the human body would suffocate or dismember at high train speeds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Early passenger trains often had to calm terrified riders with sealed curtains.

name: Submarine
visual_anchor: Stealthy matte-black nuclear submarine cruising semi-submerged through crashing ocean swells at dusk.
core_traits: Watercraft capable of independent underwater operation and navigation
Controls buoyancy using ballast tanks filled alternately with water or compressed air
Modern nuclear submarines can stay submerged for months limited only by food rations
Uses active and passive SONAR acoustic technology to detect vessels

facts_and_myths.claim: Nuclear submarines must regularly surface to replenish breathable oxygen for the crew.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Nuclear subs generate oxygen indefinitely by splitting ocean water molecules (electrolysis) and scrub carbon dioxide.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: They can remain submerged for years; the only limiting factor is food supplies for the sailors.

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern submarines do not use periscopes with glass mirrors anymore.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern attack subs use photonic optronic masts with high-definition digital cameras and infrared sensors sent to video screens.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Some modern US Navy submarine periscope masts are controlled using Xbox video game controllers.

name: Electric Car
visual_anchor: Aerodynamic electric sedan charging at a sleek glowing supercharger station at night.
core_traits: Automobile propelled by one or more electric motors powered by rechargeable lithium-ion battery packs
Produces zero direct tailpipe exhaust emissions during operation
Delivers instant peak torque from a standstill for rapid acceleration
Features regenerative braking to recapture kinetic energy into electrical power

facts_and_myths.claim: Electric cars are a brand new invention created in the 21st century.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Electric cars were invented in the 1830s and outsold gasoline cars in early 1900s New York before cheap oil took over.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ferdinand Porsche built the world's first hybrid electric car, the Lohner-Porsche, in 1900.

facts_and_myths.claim: Electric vehicles can generate electrical charge while slowing down through regenerative braking.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The electric drive motor reverses function into an alternator generator, converting braking friction into stored battery juice.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: This also drastically reduces brake pad wear compared to traditional cars.

name: Smartphone
visual_anchor: Ultra-thin bezel-less smartphone glowing in hand with an edge-to-edge OLED display and camera lenses.
core_traits: Handheld portable personal computer combining cellular telephone with internet connectivity
Operated primarily through a multi-touch capacitive glass touchscreen interface
Equipped with high-resolution digital cameras, GPS navigation, and biometric sensors
Hosts millions of software applications (apps) via digital application stores

facts_and_myths.claim: An average modern smartphone has millions of times more computing memory than the NASA Apollo 11 guidance computer.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Apollo Guidance Computer had just 4KB of RAM and 72KB of ROM; a smartphone has gigabytes of RAM, millions of times more powerful.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Apollo astronauts landed on the Moon with less computing power than a modern pocket calculator.

facts_and_myths.claim: Leaving your smartphone plugged into its charger overnight will damage and overcharge the battery.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern phones contain smart battery management chips that cut off charging current once 100% capacity is reached.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Lithium-ion batteries do experience slight aging over time from heat, but cannot be 'overcharged'.

name: Helicopter
visual_anchor: Sleek rescue helicopter hovering steadily over turbulent ocean waves under dramatic searchlights.
core_traits: Aircraft lifted and propelled by one or more horizontal overhead rotors
Capable of taking off and landing vertically without a runway
Can hover stationary in mid-air and fly backwards or sideways
Relies on a tail rotor to counteract the torque created by main rotor rotation

facts_and_myths.claim: If a helicopter engine fails completely in mid-air, it immediately drops straight down like a stone.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Helicopters can land safely without engine power using autorotation, where upward rushing air spins the blades to generate lift.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pilots practice engine-off autorotation landings regularly during flight certification.

facts_and_myths.claim: Igor Sikorsky designed the first practical single-rotor helicopter that entered mass production.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sikorsky's R-4 in 1942 established the standard single main rotor and tail anti-torque rotor configuration.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Leonardo da Vinci sketched an aerial screw ancestor of the helicopter back in the 1480s.

name: Hot Air Balloon
visual_anchor: Vibrant rainbow hot air balloon floating gracefully over misty fairy chimneys in Cappadocia at sunrise.
core_traits: Oldest successful human-carrying flight technology invented in 1783
Generates lift by heating air inside a large nylon fabric envelope with propane burners
Carries passengers and fuel tanks in an open wicker basket suspended underneath
Drifts directionally with prevailing wind currents at varying altitudes

facts_and_myths.claim: Hot air balloon pilots can steer left or right using a mechanical steering wheel.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Balloons have no rudder; pilots steer solely by ascending or descending into wind layers blowing in different directions.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Wicker is still used for baskets because it is lightweight, extremely flexible, and absorbs landing impact.

facts_and_myths.claim: The very first passengers aboard a hot air balloon were a sheep, a duck, and a rooster.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In September 1783, the Montgolfier brothers launched these three farm animals to test if living creatures could survive high altitudes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: All three animals survived the historic flight completely unharmed.

name: Blimp
visual_anchor: Massive illuminated white advertising blimp cruising smoothly above a crowded nighttime stadium.
core_traits: Non-rigid lighter-than-air aircraft that maintains its aerodynamic shape solely via internal gas pressure
Filled with non-flammable lighter-than-air helium gas to generate buoyant lift
Propelled by external engines and steered with aerodynamic tail fins and rudders
Frequently used for aerial broadcasting, surveillance, and major sporting event advertising

facts_and_myths.claim: Blimps have an internal metal skeleton frame supporting their envelope.
facts_and_myths.explanation: True blimps have zero internal skeleton; if the gas pressure drops, the envelope completely collapses.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Rigid airships with metal frames are called Zeppelins or dirigibles, not blimps.

facts_and_myths.claim: Fewer than thirty active blimps operate in the entire world today.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Blimps are expensive to operate and store, making working non-rigid blimps rarer than certified astronauts.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Goodyear's famous fleet modern airships are technically semi-rigid Zeppelins.

name: Hang Glider
visual_anchor: Colorfully paneled delta-wing hang glider soaring silently along towering coastal sea cliffs over azure waters.
core_traits: Non-motorized, foot-launched glider aircraft with a flexible delta-shaped wing
Pilot is suspended in a harness below the wing and controls flight by shifting body weight
Constructed from lightweight aluminum alloy or carbon fiber framing and ripstop dacron fabric
Maintains aloft flight by riding thermal updrafts and coastal ridge lift

facts_and_myths.claim: Hang gliders require an engine or motorized tow vehicle to stay airborne.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hang gliders are completely unpowered; experienced pilots harness natural rising warm air thermals to fly for hours.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The world distance record for a single unpowered hang glider flight exceeds 700 kilometers.

facts_and_myths.claim: NASA aerospace engineer Francis Rogallo's spacecraft recovery parachute inspired modern hang gliders.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Rogallo invented the flexible delta wing in 1948, which became the fundamental blueprint for recreational hang gliding.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Early hang gliding pioneers built their wings out of bamboo and plastic sheeting.

name: Parachute
visual_anchor: Bright multi-colored rectangular ram-air parachute canopy flared gracefully just before soft touchdown in a green dropzone.
core_traits: Device that slows the descent of an object or person falling through an atmosphere by creating aerodynamic drag
Constructed from high-tensile ripstop nylon fabric connected by suspension lines to a body harness
Modern steerable ram-air canopies act as inflatable aerofoil wings offering glide and precision steering
Essential life-saving emergency equipment for aviators and military airborne troops

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern square sport parachutes merely drop straight down without generating forward flying speed.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern ram-air square parachutes inflate into true wings that generate dynamic forward lift, flying up to 30 mph.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Parachutists can perform precision landings on targets the size of a coin.

facts_and_myths.claim: The word parachute comes from the French words 'para' meaning against and 'chute' meaning fall.
facts_and_myths.explanation: French inventor Louis-Sebastien Lenormand coined the term in 1783 when making the first witnessed parachute descent.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Lenormand made his pioneering jump from an observatory tower using two modified umbrellas.

name: Fighter Jet
visual_anchor: Sharp twin-engine supersonic fighter jet tearing through the sky with bright afterburners blazing at dusk.
core_traits: High-speed, highly maneuverable military fixed-wing aircraft designed primarily for air-to-air combat
Powered by advanced afterburning turbofan engines achieving speeds beyond Mach 2
Equipped with radar-guided air-to-air missiles, precision bombs, and high-rate autocannons
Flown by pilots wearing pressurized G-suits to withstand turns exceeding 9 times Earth gravity

facts_and_myths.claim: Fighter jet cockpits are completely silent because the plane flies faster than sound.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sound travels through the aircraft's physical metal fuselage faster than through air, so pilots clearly hear engine roar and cockpit alarms.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pilots communicate through noise-canceling headsets built inside airtight flight helmets.

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern fighter jets are aerodynamically unstable on purpose to allow lightning-fast turns.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Fly-by-wire computer flight systems make hundreds of micro-adjustments per second to control inherently unstable nimble airframes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Without computer assistance, a human pilot could not keep an unstable 5th-generation stealth jet level.

name: Supersonic Concorde
visual_anchor: Iconic slender white Concorde SST with droop nose lowered touching down smoothly on a heat-rippled tarmac.
core_traits: Pioneering turbojet-powered supersonic passenger airliner operating from 1976 to 2003
Cruised at over twice the speed of sound (Mach 2.04) at 60,000 feet altitude
Featured an iconic delta wing design and a mechanically drooping nose for runway visibility
Crossed the Atlantic Ocean from London/Paris to New York in under 3.5 hours

facts_and_myths.claim: Concorde stretched up to 10 inches longer in mid-flight due to atmospheric friction heating.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Frictional heating at Mach 2 warmed the aluminum airframe up to 127 degrees Celsius, causing thermal expansion.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Flight engineers could put their hand into an expansion gap between the cockpit console and bulkhead during flight.

facts_and_myths.claim: Concorde passengers could see the curvature of the Earth from their cabin windows.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Cruising at 60,000 feet (twice normal airliner altitude), the planetary curve and deep indigo-black stratosphere were distinctly visible.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Concorde flew faster than the rotation of the Earth, arriving in New York earlier local time than when it departed London.

name: Cargo Plane
visual_anchor: Colossal multi-engine air freighter with its hinged nose opened upward swallowing oversized heavy shipping containers.
core_traits: Fixed-wing aircraft designed primarily for transporting palletized cargo, freight, and oversized machinery
Features a wide cavernous fuselage without passenger windows and reinforced freight deck flooring
Equipped with built-in roller tracks and large upward-opening nose or tail loading ramps
Operates massive global supply chain routes for express air express and logistics networks

facts_and_myths.claim: Cargo planes are simply retired passenger planes with passenger seats unscrewed and removed.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Purpose-built air freighters feature reinforced titanium/steel cargo floor beams, specialized loading doors, and fire suppression systems.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Antonov An-225 Mriya was the heaviest aircraft ever built, capable of hauling 250 tons of freight.

facts_and_myths.claim: Air cargo handles less than 1% of world trade volume by weight, but over 35% of world trade by economic value.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Air freight is reserved for high-value, time-critical goods like electronics, pharmaceuticals, and luxury items.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Fresh flowers and live zoo animals regularly travel in temperature-regulated air cargo holds.

name: Seaplane
visual_anchor: Rugged yellow floatplane throwing white spray across a pristine glassy mountain lake surrounded by pine forests.
core_traits: Powered fixed-wing aircraft capable of taking off and landing on water surfaces
Fitted with large pontoon floats mounted beneath the fuselage instead of traditional wheels
Provides critical transport access to remote island archipelagos, wilderness lakes, and coastal bays
Equipped with corrosion-resistant marine coatings and retractable water rudders

facts_and_myths.claim: A seaplane and a flying boat are identical aircraft engineering terms.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Floatplanes use pontoon floats attached under a regular fuselage; flying boats have a boat-shaped hull that sits directly in water.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many floatplanes are amphibious, with wheels tucked inside the pontoons for runway landings.

facts_and_myths.claim: Pilots require a specialized marine navigation rating to fly seaplanes because maritime right-of-way rules apply on water.
facts_and_myths.explanation: When waterborne, seaplanes are legally classified as power vessels and must obey international maritime navigation rules.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Seaplanes must yield the right of way to sailboats and canoes when taxiing on lakes.

name: Glider
visual_anchor: Ultra-sleek white sailplane with extraordinarily long narrow wings cutting silently through crystal clear blue mountain skies.
core_traits: Unpowered heavier-than-air fixed-wing aircraft sustained solely by aerodynamic reaction on its wings
Features extremely high aspect ratio wings designed for maximum lift-to-drag glide ratios
Launched into the sky by an airplane tow line or a high-speed ground winch cable
Soars for hundreds of miles by climbing natural rising air currents such as thermals and ridge waves

facts_and_myths.claim: Gliders can stay airborne for over 10 hours and travel over 1,000 miles without an engine.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Skilled glider pilots hop between rising thermal updrafts in the atmosphere to cover enormous distances.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The world distance record for a glider flight is over 3,000 kilometers.

facts_and_myths.claim: If a glider encounters completely still air without thermals, it immediately crashes into the ground.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Gliders maintain forward speed by descending gently, turning potential energy into kinetic energy with a glide ratio up to 60 to 1.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A top-tier glider can travel 60 kilometers horizontally for every single kilometer of altitude lost.

name: Biplane
visual_anchor: Classic wooden and fabric yellow biplane performing an aerial loop with dual wings connected by gleaming wire struts.
core_traits: Fixed-wing aircraft featuring two stacked wings, one placed above the other
Dominant design during the early aviation era, World War I, and 1920s barnstorming
Stacked wing architecture provided high structural strength with lightweight wood and fabric
Renowned for exceptional low-speed agility and short takeoff distances

facts_and_myths.claim: The Wright brothers' historic Flyer 1 in 1903 was a biplane.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Orville and Wilbur Wright chose the dual-wing truss configuration because it offered superior strength-to-weight ratio.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Modern aerobatic display planes like the Pitts Special still use biplane wings for rapid roll rates.

facts_and_myths.claim: Biplanes are naturally faster than single-wing monoplanes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Biplanes produce significantly more aerodynamic drag due to wing interference and support struts, making them slower.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Monoplanes replaced biplanes in the 1930s as all-metal stressed skin designs eliminated the need for external struts.

name: Stealth Bomber
visual_anchor: Sinister matte-black flying-wing stealth bomber cruising silently across the moonlit sky with zero visible rudders.
core_traits: Long-range strategic heavy military bomber built with low-observable stealth technology
Unique pure flying wing shape with no vertical tail fin or fuselage protrusions
Coated in radar-absorbent materials to present a radar cross-section smaller than a small bird
Capable of penetrating dense anti-aircraft air defenses to deploy precision ordnance

facts_and_myths.claim: Stealth bombers are completely invisible to the human eye when flying overhead.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Stealth aircraft are visible to human eyesight; stealth refers strictly to radar, infrared, acoustic, and electromagnetic signatures.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: To reduce visual detection from the ground, they fly at high altitudes and use anti-reflective matte gray paint.

facts_and_myths.claim: The B-2 Stealth Bomber is the most expensive production aircraft in aviation history.
facts_and_myths.explanation: With procurement and development costs included, each B-2 Spirit cost over 2 billion US dollars.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Only 21 operational B-2 bombers were ever constructed.

name: Gyrocopter
visual_anchor: Compact open-cockpit gyrocopter cruising low over sandy coastlines with its unpowered free-spinning rotor blades.
core_traits: Rotorcraft with an unpowered overhead rotor that spins freely via aerodynamic autorotation
Propelled forward by an independent engine-driven pusher or tractor propeller
Invented in 1923 by Spanish engineer Juan de la Cierva to prevent aircraft stalls
Cannot hover in completely calm air but can land in astonishingly short distances

facts_and_myths.claim: A gyrocopter's top rotor is powered by an engine throughout the entire flight.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The main rotor has no engine connection during flight; forward motion pushes air upward through the blades to spin them naturally.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Because the rotor is always in autorotation, gyrocopters cannot stall in the traditional aviation sense.

facts_and_myths.claim: Gyrocopters can land safely even if their forward thrust engine fails.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Since the lift rotor already operates in permanent autorotation, a dead engine simply causes the craft to glide to a gentle landing.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A gyrocopter was famously featured in the James Bond movie 'You Only Live Twice' as 'Little Nellie'.

name: Tiltrotor Aircraft
visual_anchor: Military tiltrotor aircraft rotating its massive wingtip proprotors forward from vertical hover to horizontal high-speed flight.
core_traits: Aircraft that generates lift and propulsion using proprotors mounted on tilting wingtip nacelles
Combines the vertical takeoff, landing, and hovering capabilities of a helicopter with airplane speed
Transitions in mid-flight between helicopter mode and turboprop airplane mode
Cruises twice as fast and twice as far as conventional rotary-wing helicopters

facts_and_myths.claim: If one wingtip engine fails on a tiltrotor, the aircraft flips over immediately.
facts_and_myths.explanation: An interconnected drive shaft runs through the wings, allowing either engine to power both proprotors simultaneously.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The drive shaft spins at over 6,000 RPM inside the aircraft's upper wing.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Bell Boeing V-22 Osprey was the first operational military tiltrotor in world history.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Entering service in 2007 with the US Marine Corps, it revolutionized amphibious troop transport and long-range rescue.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Its wings can fold parallel to the fuselage and rotor blades tuck in for compact aircraft carrier storage.

name: Flying Boat
visual_anchor: Majestic vintage four-engine passenger flying boat skimming across harbor waters leaving a long foaming white wake.
core_traits: Fixed-wing seaplane with a buoyant, boat-shaped fuselage that rests directly in the water
Golden Age transoceanic luxury airliners such as the legendary Pan American Boeing 314 Clippers
Stabilized on the water surface by small sponsons or retractable wingtip floats
Enabled international passenger air travel before modern long paved concrete runways existed

facts_and_myths.claim: Howard Hughes' famous Spruce Goose was the largest flying boat ever constructed by wingspan.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Hughes H-4 Hercules had a staggering 320-foot wingspan and was built almost entirely of laminated birch wood.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Spruce Goose flew only once, in November 1947, staying aloft for roughly one minute.

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern aviation no longer uses flying boats for any purpose.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Giant modern amphibious flying boats like the Canadair CL-415 and ShinMaywa US-2 serve as vital water bombers and sea rescue craft.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Water bomber flying boats can scoop 6,000 liters of lake water into their belly tanks in just 12 seconds.

name: Ultralight Aircraft
visual_anchor: Minimalist tubular frame ultralight trike with a buzzing rear pusher propeller cruising low over golden farmland.
core_traits: Extremely lightweight, simple 1- or 2-seat recreational aircraft operating under relaxed regulatory rules
Powered by a small high-output two-stroke or four-stroke gasoline engine
Operates with very low stall speeds and requires only a small grass strip for takeoff and landing
Built from open aluminum tubing, Dacron sailcloth wings, and minimal flight instrumentation

facts_and_myths.claim: In the United States, single-seat ultralight aircraft do not require an FAA pilot's license to fly.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Under FAA Part 103, ultralights weighing under 254 pounds empty with limited fuel capacity require no license or registration.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Despite no legal license requirement, professional training is strongly recommended for safety.

facts_and_myths.claim: Ultralights can fly through clouds and controlled commercial airport airspace anytime.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Ultralights are strictly restricted to daylight visual meteorological conditions (VFR) and prohibited from congested airport airspace.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ultralight pilots often use ballistic emergency parachutes that deploy a rocket to lower the whole aircraft.

name: Crop Duster
visual_anchor: Rugged low-wing crop duster skimming barely ten feet above sprawling corn rows releasing an even mist of fertilizer.
core_traits: Specialized agricultural fixed-wing airplane or helicopter designed for aerial application of seed and fertilizer
Equipped with large chemical hopper tanks and under-wing spray boom nozzle bars
Flies at extremely low altitudes (5 to 15 feet above crops) requiring exceptional pilot precision
Reinforced cockpits with rollover protection and forward-impact crumple zones

facts_and_myths.claim: Crop dusters still spray dry arsenic and lead dust like in early 1920s agriculture.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern agricultural planes spray liquid bio-fertilizers, targeted pesticides, or even drop rice and cover crop seeds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The nickname 'crop duster' stuck from early trials in 1921 when pilots dusted peach trees with lead arsenate powder.

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern agricultural aircraft use high-precision GPS lightbars to spray fields with inch-level accuracy.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Satellite GPS guidance guides pilots along exact parallel swathes to prevent overlapping or missed patches of crops.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Modern agricultural airplanes like the Air Tractor are powered by massive 1,400 horsepower Pratt & Whitney turboprop engines.

name: Aerial Firefighting Plane
visual_anchor: Heavy red-and-white firefighting air tanker banking hard through billowing smoke to drop a massive ribbon of crimson retardant.
core_traits: Specialized fixed-wing aircraft modified to drop thousands of gallons of water or chemical fire retardant on forest wildfires
Features pressurized internal belly tank systems and rapid emergency discharge doors
Drops crimson-colored retardant ahead of wildfire frontlines to starve advancing flames of fuel
Flies perilous low-altitude missions through intense thermal updrafts, turbulence, and dense smoke

facts_and_myths.claim: The bright red retardant dropped by firefighting planes is pure toxic chemical poison.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Fire retardant is roughly 85% water, 10% fertilizer (ammonium phosphate), and red iron oxide dye so ground crews can see drop boundaries.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The red dye fades away naturally when exposed to sunlight and rainfall.

facts_and_myths.claim: Converted Boeing 747 'SuperTankers' could drop nearly 20,000 gallons of retardant in a single pass.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The 747 SuperTanker was the world's largest firefighting aircraft, carrying massive pressurized water tanks inside its main deck.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It could lay down a retardant line 3 kilometers long in just under 20 seconds.

name: Jetpack
visual_anchor: Futuristic pilot clad in a titanium-fiber suit hovering effortlessly twenty feet above water powered by arm-mounted jet turbines.
core_traits: Wearable personal propulsion device strapped to an operator's back or limbs to allow individual flight
Powered by miniature high-thrust gas turbine jet engines or high-pressure hydrogen peroxide rocket thrusters
Pilots control direction, pitch, and altitude by varying body posture and hand-held throttle throttles
Operates with very limited flight endurance typically lasting 5 to 10 minutes per fuel load

facts_and_myths.claim: The classic Bell Rocket Belt used by the US military in the 1960s could fly for over an hour.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The rocket belt could only carry enough hydrogen peroxide propellant for about 20 to 30 seconds of flight.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It famously appeared in the 1965 James Bond film 'Thunderball'.

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern jet suits developed by Gravity Industries produce over 1,000 horsepower from micro-jet engines.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern suits use five micro-turbines (two on each arm and one on the back) capable of exceeding 80 mph.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Emergency medical and mountain rescue services have successfully tested jet suits for rapid peak rescue.

name: Paraglider
visual_anchor: Curved colorful paraglider wing floating high above a dramatic snowcapped Alpine valley with green pastures below.
core_traits: Foot-launched, steerable glider aircraft with no rigid primary structure
Features an inflatable ram-air airfoil cell canopy made of non-porous ripstop fabric
Pilot sits upright or reclined in a comfortable harness suspended beneath dozens of lines
Can be packed compactly inside a medium backpack weighing under 10 kilograms

facts_and_myths.claim: A paraglider and a skydiver's parachute are practically identical pieces of gear.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A parachute is designed to open reliably during a violent 120 mph freefall; a paraglider is a high-efficiency soaring wing launched gently from hills.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Opening a paraglider in freefall would rip the lightweight lines and destroy the canopy.

facts_and_myths.claim: Paraglider pilots can stay airborne for hundreds of miles using thermal columns of warm rising air.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Just like birds of prey, cross-country paragliders circle inside rising thermal columns to climb thousands of feet.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The world straight-distance paragliding record exceeds 580 kilometers across Brazil.

name: Wingsuit
visual_anchor: Fearless wingsuit proximity flyer soaring at 120 mph through a razor-thin rocky mountain gorge.
core_traits: Specially tailored aerodynamic jumpsuit featuring fabric membranes stretched between the legs and under the arms
Inflates during high-speed forward fall to transform the human body into a gliding airfoil
Increases the horizontal glide distance of a skydiver while drastically reducing vertical descent speed
Requires deploying a traditional sport parachute to land safely on the ground

facts_and_myths.claim: Wingsuit pilots can safely land directly on their feet without a parachute.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Wingsuits fly forward at over 100 mph and still descend at 30 to 40 mph, making an unassisted ground landing lethal.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In 2012, stuntman Gary Connery landed safely without a chute by aiming into a 350-foot runway of cardboard boxes.

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern wingsuits can achieve a glide ratio of 3 to 1 or better.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Advanced wingsuit pilots can travel three feet forward horizontally for every single foot of vertical altitude lost.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Wingsuit designs were directly inspired by the aerodynamic membranes of flying squirrels.

name: Zeppelin
visual_anchor: Enormous silver rigid airship with illuminated passenger observation windows gliding majestically over a 1930s city.
core_traits: Type of rigid airship pioneered by German Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin in the early 1900s
Constructed with a vast lightweight internal duralumin structural skeleton covered in treated fabric
Contains multiple independent internal gas cells filled with buoyant lifting gas
Provided the world's first commercial transatlantic luxury passenger air service

facts_and_myths.claim: Zeppelins and blimps have the exact same structural design.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Zeppelins have a rigid internal metal frame that maintains shape even when completely empty of gas, whereas blimps collapse.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Graf Zeppelin flew over 1 million miles and completed a complete circumnavigation of the globe in 1929.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Hindenburg disaster in 1937 brought an abrupt end to the golden age of passenger rigid airships.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The tragic hydrogen fire in New Jersey destroyed public trust in hydrogen airships and catalyzed the switch to airplanes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Hindenburg was originally designed for helium, but the US embargo forced Germany to use flammable hydrogen.

name: Spy Plane
visual_anchor: Sleek titanium-black supersonic reconnaissance aircraft cruising at Mach 3 in the near-space stratosphere with twin shock cones.
core_traits: High-altitude military aircraft designed to gather intelligence, aerial photography, and electronic signals
Iconic airframes include the high-flying U-2 glider-jet and the Mach 3.2 titanium SR-71 Blackbird
Cruises at altitudes exceeding 70,000 to 85,000 feet, well above commercial air corridors
Flown by pilots wearing pressurized full astronaut pressure suits with pure oxygen

facts_and_myths.claim: The SR-71 Blackbird intentionally leaked fuel while parked on the runway before takeoff.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Its titanium skin panels only sealed tightly when heated and expanded by supersonic atmospheric friction at Mach 3.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: No SR-71 was ever shot down by enemy missiles because its standard evasive maneuver was simply accelerating faster.

facts_and_myths.claim: Spy planes became completely obsolete immediately after the launch of the first spy satellites.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Satellites have fixed predictable orbits; spy planes can be dispatched anywhere on short notice to loiter and monitor dynamic crises.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The venerable U-2 spy plane first flew in 1955 and still flies operational missions today.

name: Spaceplane
visual_anchor: Futuristic white spaceplane with feathered tail booms gliding back into Earth atmosphere through glowing blue sky.
core_traits: Hybrid vehicle that operates as an aircraft in Earth atmosphere and as a spacecraft in outer space
Equipped with aerodynamic wings and control surfaces for unpowered glide landings on conventional runways
Propelled into space by rocket engines or air-launched from a mother transport carrier aircraft
Pioneered by experimental vehicles like the X-15, SpaceShipOne, and the autonomous military X-37B

facts_and_myths.claim: SpaceShipOne won the 10 million dollar Ansari X Prize in 2004 as the first private crewed suborbital spaceplane.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Designed by Burt Rutan, it flew twice to over 100 kilometers altitude within two weeks to claim the prize.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It used a unique 'feathering' wing mechanism that folded the tail upward to safely auto-stabilize reentry.

facts_and_myths.claim: All spaceplanes can take off from a regular airport runway directly using only standard jet engines.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Reaching orbital speed requires enormous rocket propellant mass; most spaceplanes require rocket boosters or carrier launch planes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The robotic Boeing X-37B spaceplane has spent over 900 consecutive days in Earth orbit before landing on a runway.

name: Air Ambulance Helicopter
visual_anchor: Bright red medical emergency helicopter landing on a rooftop hospital helipad with paramedics rushing an intensive care stretcher.
core_traits: Helicopter equipped with advanced life-support medical equipment and specialized trauma flight crews
Transports critically ill or injured patients rapidly from accident scenes to specialized trauma centers
Equipped with portable ventilators, cardiac monitors, defibrillators, and emergency blood supplies
Can land on highway crash sites, remote mountain terrain, and hospital rooftop helipads

facts_and_myths.claim: Air ambulances only transport patients and do not carry medical doctors or flight nurses.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Air ambulance crews typically include flight paramedics, critical care nurses, and specialized emergency trauma physicians.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: They function as flying intensive care units capable of emergency blood transfusions and minor surgical airway procedures.

facts_and_myths.claim: Medevac helicopters dramatically increase survival rates for trauma patients during the critical 'golden hour'.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The golden hour refers to the first 60 minutes after severe traumatic injury where rapid definitive care saves lives.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Helicopter medical transport was first popularized during the Korean and Vietnam wars.

name: Bush Plane
visual_anchor: High-wing wilderness bush plane with gigantic low-pressure tundra tires perched on an Alaskan river gravel bar.
core_traits: Rugged general aviation airplane designed to access remote wilderness areas without paved runways
Features high wings for visibility and oversized low-pressure balloon tundra tires to land on riverbeds and mud
Engineered for Short Takeoff and Landing (STOL) performance over tight tree canopies
Often equipped with swappable wheel skis for snow operations or pontoons for glacial lakes

facts_and_myths.claim: Bush planes need at least a mile of flat paved tarmac to take off.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Equipped with high-lift flaps and powerful engines, many STOL bush planes can take off in under 100 feet of gravel.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: STOL bush plane competition pilots can take off in distances shorter than the length of the plane itself.

facts_and_myths.claim: Tundra tires are inflated to very low pressures to absorb impacts from boulders and logs.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Inflated to just 4 to 8 PSI, the massive soft tires cushion brutal rough-field landings without damaging the landing gear.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Bush planes are the sole lifeline for many isolated indigenous communities throughout Alaska and northern Canada.

name: Glider Tow Plane
visual_anchor: Sturdy taildragger airplane pulling a sleek sailplane behind it on a long yellow towline above green patchwork fields.
core_traits: High-power single-engine aircraft specifically rigged to tow unpowered gliders into the air
Fitted with a rear-mounted tow release hook and heavy-duty steel or nylon towline mechanism
Climbs steep ascents while hauling a glider to an altitude with promising thermal activity
Features upgraded engine cooling systems to prevent overheating during slow high-power climbs

facts_and_myths.claim: In an emergency, only the tow plane pilot has the ability to release the tow cable.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Both the tow plane pilot and the glider pilot have independent quick-release levers to sever the tow cable immediately.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tow releases use a standardized mechanical ring coupling called a Schweizer release.

facts_and_myths.claim: During World War II, military tow planes pulled large gliders loaded with dozens of combat troops across the English Channel.
facts_and_myths.explanation: C-47 transports towed massive wooden Horsa and Waco troop gliders into Normandy on D-Day.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Gliders could land silently behind enemy lines without engine noise giving away their position.

name: Military Transport Plane
visual_anchor: Massive four-turboprop military airlifter performing a rough tactical dirt runway landing kicking up a huge dust cloud.
core_traits: Heavy military aircraft engineered to airlift combat troops, armored vehicles, and humanitarian relief supplies
Equipped with a large rear cargo ramp that allows airdropping paratroopers and heavy palletized equipment in flight
Capable of operating from unprepared dirt strips, sandy beaches, and icy Antarctic runways
Exemplified by legendary workhorses like the Lockheed C-130 Hercules and Boeing C-17 Globemaster

facts_and_myths.claim: The C-130 Hercules holds the record for the longest continuous production run of any military aircraft in history.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In continuous production since 1954, more than 2,500 C-130 aircraft have been delivered to over 60 nations.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Grandfathers, fathers, and sons have served as pilots on the same C-130 airframe.

facts_and_myths.claim: Military transports cannot land on unimproved dirt or unpaved runways without breaking their landing gear.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Tactical airlifters are built with multi-wheel heavy-duty landing gear designed specifically to disperse weight over soft dirt.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A C-130 once made 29 successful touch-and-go landings on the deck of an aircraft carrier without arresting wires.

name: Drone
visual_anchor: Matte-carbon quadcopter drone hovering steadily in the wind with a 4K camera gimbal tilted down over a cityscape.
core_traits: Unmanned aircraft guided autonomously by onboard computers or operated via remote radio control
Equipped with multi-rotor propellers that vary rotational speed for dynamic pitch, yaw, and roll control
Fitted with GPS positioning, obstacle avoidance sensors, and stabilized camera gimbals
Used extensively for aerial cinematography, agriculture, structural inspection, search-and-rescue, and delivery

facts_and_myths.claim: All drones require a human pilot constantly holding a control stick to stay balanced in the air.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Drones use onboard gyroscopes, accelerometers, and optical flow sensors to auto-level and hover in place hands-free.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: If radio signal is lost, modern drones automatically fly home and land via GPS Return-to-Home failsafes.

facts_and_myths.claim: Drones are used in modern light shows to replace fireworks with synchronized aerial animations.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Thousands of LED-equipped drones fly in coordinated swarms programmed by a single master computer.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Swarms of over 5,000 synchronized drones have set Guinness World Records for aerial light displays.

name: Solar-Powered Airplane
visual_anchor: Ultra-lightweight solar airplane with an immense wingspan covered in shimmering blue photovoltaic cells cruising above clouds.
core_traits: Electric aircraft powered directly by sunlight collected by solar panels mounted on its upper wings
Stores surplus solar energy in lithium polymer batteries during the day to sustain flight through the night
Engineered with an immense glider-like wingspan wider than a Boeing 747 but weighing as little as a family car
Achieved historical milestone in 2016 when Solar Impulse 2 completed a zero-fuel round-the-world circumnavigation

facts_and_myths.claim: Solar-powered airplanes cannot fly at night because the sun is down.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They store daytime solar energy in high-capacity onboard batteries and glide down slowly from high altitudes overnight.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Solar Impulse 2 flew continuously across the Pacific Ocean for 5 consecutive days and nights without landing.

facts_and_myths.claim: Solar Impulse 2's wingspan was 72 meters, which is wider than a Boeing 747 commercial jetliner.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Its massive wing held over 17,000 solar cells while the entire carbon-fiber aircraft weighed only 2.3 tons.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Its electric motors operated with an energy efficiency exceeding 94%.

name: Microjet
visual_anchor: Tiny needle-nosed personal microjet jetting through the sky at 300 mph with an engine barely larger than a watermelon.
core_traits: Extremely compact, lightweight single-seat or two-seat jet-propelled aircraft
Powered by a miniature turbojet engine that delivers high thrust with a tiny airframe footprint
Popularized by the kit-built Bede BD-5J, famously featured in airshows and movies
Offers high-speed aerobatic maneuverability and jet performance at a fraction of business jet size

facts_and_myths.claim: The BD-5J Microjet holds the Guinness World Record for the world's smallest jet aircraft.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Weighing just 358 pounds empty with a 17-foot wingspan, it is recognized as the world's lightest jet.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: James Bond famously piloted one through an airplane hangar in the opening scene of 'Octopussy'.

facts_and_myths.claim: Microjets are so small that they do not need retractable landing gear.
facts_and_myths.explanation: To minimize drag and achieve speeds exceeding 300 mph, microjets use fully retractable tricycle landing gear.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The microjet's fuel tanks are built directly into the hollow wings.

name: Aerobatic Plane
visual_anchor: Sleek bright red aerobatic monoplane flying inverted inches above a racing pylon leaving a thick spiral smoke trail.
core_traits: Specialized high-performance aircraft built to perform extreme aerial maneuvers, loops, and barrel rolls
Engineered with symmetrical wing airfoils that fly equally well right-side-up or completely upside-down
Reinforced carbon composite structures capable of withstanding extreme stresses of plus and minus 10 Gs
Equipped with inverted fuel and oil injection systems to keep the engine running smoothly during negative G maneuvers

facts_and_myths.claim: Standard passenger airplanes can safely fly inverted upside-down indefinitely just like stunt planes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Passenger planes have asymmetrical wings and gravity-fed fuel systems that would stall engines and starve oil systems within seconds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Aerobatic planes have special flop-tube fuel pickups that swing with gravity inside the tank.

facts_and_myths.claim: Red Bull Air Race aerobatic planes can roll 360 degrees horizontally in under one second.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Competition planes like the Edge 540 boast roll rates exceeding 420 degrees per second.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Stunt pilots use colored mineral oil injected directly into the engine exhaust pipe to create aerobatic smoke trails.

name: Vintage Triplane
visual_anchor: Iconic crimson three-winged Fokker Triplane diving steeply through World War I clouds with rotary engine humming.
core_traits: Early fighter aircraft featuring three stacked main wings mounted vertically on the fuselage
Achieved immortal fame during World War I as the aircraft flown by the 'Red Baron' Manfred von Richthofen
Offered an extraordinary rate of climb and unmatched dogfight turning agility at low speeds
Powered by a whirling rotary radial engine where the cylinders spun around a stationary crankshaft

facts_and_myths.claim: Manfred von Richthofen, the Red Baron, scored all 80 of his aerial victories in the Fokker Triplane.
facts_and_myths.explanation: He scored only 19 of his 80 kills in the Dr.I triplane; the majority were won in Albatros biplanes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: His red triplane became an international cultural icon despite his short operational time in it.

facts_and_myths.claim: In rotary aircraft engines of that era, the engine cylinders spun around together with the propeller.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Oberursel rotary engine spun its entire 9-cylinder block to aid air-cooling, creating immense gyroscopic turning forces.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The gyroscopic force made triplanes turn right with lightning speed, but turning left took deliberate muscular effort.

name: VTOL Jet
visual_anchor: Modern F-35B stealth jet hovering motionlessly in mid-air over a naval deck before setting down vertically like a feather.
core_traits: Military jet aircraft capable of Vertical Take-Off and Landing without requiring a paved runway or catapult
Pioneered by the British Harrier Jump Jet using rotating engine thrust-vectoring nozzles
Modern variants use downward lift-fans driven by a central drive shaft combined with a swivel exhaust nozzle
Enables high-performance jet operations from small amphibious assault ships and dispersed road clearings

facts_and_myths.claim: VTOL jets take off vertically on every single operational combat mission.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Taking off vertically consumes vast amounts of fuel and severely limits weapon payload; they usually perform Short Take-Off and Vertical Landing (STOVL).
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Running takeoffs along a short ramp allow the jet to lift thousands of pounds of extra bombs and fuel.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Harrier jump jet could rotate its exhaust nozzles forward in mid-flight to decelerate violently in dogfights.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Called 'viffing' (vectoring in forward flight), pilots used this combat trick to cause pursuing enemy jets to overshoot.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Royal Air Force demonstrated this tactical move during the 1982 Falklands War.

name: Search and Rescue Helicopter
visual_anchor: Bright orange Coast Guard rescue helicopter lowering a rescue swimmer into stormy ocean swells next to a stranded vessel.
core_traits: Specialized multi-mission maritime helicopter equipped for locating and rescuing people in distress
Features high-power variable-speed electric rescue winches, rescue baskets, and search radar
Equipped with Forward-Looking Infrared (FLIR) cameras that detect human body heat in freezing seas
Crewed by pilots, flight mechanics, and trained emergency rescue swimmers

facts_and_myths.claim: SAR helicopters cannot fly into fog or zero-visibility conditions at sea.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern SAR helicopters feature digital 4-axis auto-hover autopilots linked to radar and GPS that lock onto hover points automatically.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The computer keeps the helicopter perfectly motionless over turbulent waves even if the pilot lets go of controls.

facts_and_myths.claim: Coast Guard rescue swimmers must jump directly into freezing 30-foot seas from hovering helicopters.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Rescue swimmers deploy via high jumps or winch cable into icy water to secure survivors into rescue harnesses.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The motto of US Coast Guard aviation rescue swimmers is 'So Others May Live'.

name: Heavy-Lift Helicopter
visual_anchor: Colossal twin-rotor tandem helicopter hoisting a heavy military bulldozer suspended on steel cables over rugged mountains.
core_traits: Giant helicopter engineered specifically to transport outsized external cargo, heavy machinery, and artillery
Iconic models include the tandem-rotor Boeing CH-47 Chinook and the skeletal Sikorsky S-64 Skycrane
Equipped with ventral cargo hooks capable of lifting payloads weighing 20,000 to 44,000 pounds
Vital for erecting remote electrical transmission towers, logging, and heavy construction

facts_and_myths.claim: Tandem-rotor helicopters like the Chinook do not have or need an anti-torque tail rotor.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The two huge main rotors spin in opposite directions (counter-rotating), perfectly canceling each other's torque.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Because 100% of engine power goes into vertical lift rather than tail anti-torque, tandem helicopters are exceptionally efficient.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Mil Mi-26 is large enough to carry an entire commercial airliner inside its cargo hold.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Russian Mi-26 is the largest production helicopter ever built, capable of lifting an 82-passenger jetliner.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Its cargo hold has comparable volume to a C-130 Hercules transport airplane.

name: Reconnaissance Balloon
visual_anchor: Massive tethered aerodynamic aerostat balloon floating thousands of feet above the desert carrying high-tech surveillance radar.
core_traits: Lighter-than-air tethered or free-floating gas envelope carrying intelligence sensors and communication relays
Historically deployed from the American Civil War and World War I to observe artillery fire and enemy troop movements
Modern stratospheric variants float in near-space at 60,000 to 100,000 feet carrying solar-powered sensor arrays
Provides persistent, long-duration monitoring over fixed territories at far lower cost than satellites

facts_and_myths.claim: Observation balloons in World War I were the first military aircraft where observers were equipped with parachutes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because balloons were stationary targets filled with flammable hydrogen, observers had parachutes years before fighter pilots did.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Attacking enemy observation balloons was among the most dangerous missions for fighter aces due to heavy anti-aircraft rings.

facts_and_myths.claim: Stratospheric spy balloons have no way to control their direction and simply drift randomly forever.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern high-altitude balloons pump air in and out to adjust buoyancy, moving up and down into wind currents traveling in desired directions.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: High-tech steering algorithms allow balloons to hover over a single geographic zone for weeks.

name: Attack Helicopter
visual_anchor: Fierce armored AH-64 Apache gunship hovering low over a ridgeline with its 30mm chin autocannon tracking target lock.
core_traits: Armored military rotary-wing aircraft designed specifically to engage ground targets and armored vehicles
Features tandem two-person cockpits (pilot in back, co-pilot/gunner in front) with heavy Kevlar/titanium armor
Armed with chin-mounted 30mm chain guns, laser-guided anti-tank missiles, and unguided rocket pods
Equipped with mast-mounted fire-control radar to detect dozens of enemy targets while concealed behind tree lines

facts_and_myths.claim: The Apache gunner's 30mm nose autocannon automatically moves to track wherever the pilot turns their eye.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Helmet Mounted Display System links the pilot's helmet sensors directly to the gun turret, pointing where the pilot looks.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pilots undergo intense mental training to view two different visual feeds simultaneously in each eye.

facts_and_myths.claim: Attack helicopters cannot fly in heavy rain or at nighttime.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Equipped with forward-looking infrared (FLIR) thermal vision and millimeter-wave radar, they excel at nighttime and all-weather combat.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Thermal cameras can detect the residual heat of footsteps on ground surfaces from miles away.

name: Sailplane
visual_anchor: Graceful carbon-fiber sailplane banking steeply along a sunlit Alpine ridge with wings flexed upward in lift.
core_traits: Specialized high-performance glider designed for competition distance, speed, and soaring cross-country
Constructed entirely of ultra-smooth glass-fiber and carbon-fiber composite materials
Carries water ballast in internal wing tanks to increase penetration speed between rising thermals
Dumps water ballast before landing to minimize touchdown speed and landing rollout

facts_and_myths.claim: Sailplane pilots intentionally fill their hollow wings with hundreds of pounds of water before flying.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Water ballast adds weight, increasing the speed at which the glider achieves its optimal glide ratio through sinking air.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: When thermals weaken in the afternoon, pilots open jettison valves to dump the water in seconds.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sailplanes cannot fly over high mountain peaks because there is not enough air.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Using atmospheric mountain wave lift, the Perlan 2 sailplane soared to over 76,000 feet in 2018, higher than U-2 spy planes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: At 76,000 feet, sailplane pilots must breathe pressurized pure oxygen and wear pressurized space suits.

name: Experimental Rocket Plane
visual_anchor: Bullet-shaped orange Bell X-1 dropping from the bomb bay of a B-29 bomber before igniting four rocket chambers into supersonic flight.
core_traits: Research aircraft powered by liquid-propellant rocket engines rather than air-breathing jet engines
Designed to explore extreme aerodynamic frontiers, supersonic flight, and hypersonic atmospheric entry
Chuck Yeager flew the rocket-powered Bell X-1 on October 14, 1947, becoming the first human to break the sound barrier
The hypersonic X-15 reached Mach 6.7 (4,520 mph) and altitudes over 60 miles, earning pilots astronaut wings

facts_and_myths.claim: Breaking the sound barrier in 1947 created an impenetrable physical 'sound wall' that destroyed aircraft.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Early planes encountered violent shockwave buffeting, but sleek aerodynamic shaping allowed the X-1 to punch smoothly through.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Chuck Yeager flew the historic supersonic flight with two broken ribs concealed from his commanders.

facts_and_myths.claim: The North American X-15 still holds the official world record for the highest speed ever reached by a crewed powered aircraft.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Pilot Pete Knight achieved Mach 6.7 in 1967, a crewed aircraft speed record that stands unbroken after more than half a century.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The X-15's outer skin was made of heat-resistant nickel-chrome alloy called Inconel X.

name: Skydiving Plane
visual_anchor: Twin-turboprop jump plane climbing rapidly over the coast with its side roll-up door open as skydivers prepare to leap.
core_traits: General aviation aircraft modified specifically to ferry sport skydivers to jump altitudes of 10,000 to 18,000 feet
Features stripped-down lightweight interiors with bench seating and a roll-up Plexiglas jump door
Fitted with external handrails, footpegs, and red-to-green jump light signal systems
Engineered for rapid climb rates to altitude and steep descending spirals back to the runway

facts_and_myths.claim: Skydiving planes climb slowly and take over an hour to reach jump altitude.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern turboprop jump ships like the Super Twin Otter climb to 14,000 feet in just 10 to 15 minutes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: After drop-off, the plane dives down with flaps and beta prop pitch, often beating the parachutists back to the ground.

facts_and_myths.claim: Jump planes operate without passenger seats to maximize skydiver capacity and speed up exits.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Seats are replaced with floor mats or narrow straddle benches so jumpers wearing bulky parachute rigs fit comfortably.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A standard Twin Otter can carry up to 22 jumpers per flight.

name: Aerial Refueling Tanker
visual_anchor: Huge tanker jet extending a rigid flying boom downward into the refueling receptacle of a trailing fighter jet at 30,000 feet.
core_traits: Military tanker aircraft converted to transfer aviation fuel to other aircraft in mid-flight
Utilizes a rigid steerable 'flying boom' controlled by a boom operator or a flexible 'probe-and-drogue' hose basket
Carries hundreds of thousands of pounds of jet fuel inside internal fuselage and wing fuel bladders
Multiplies the combat range and flight endurance of bombers, fighters, and surveillance aircraft worldwide

facts_and_myths.claim: Aerial refueling can transfer up to 1,000 gallons of fuel per minute between planes flying at 500 mph.
facts_and_myths.explanation: High-pressure fuel pumps push aviation kerosene through the flying boom fast enough to fill a fighter jet in minutes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Refueling requires flying formations spaced only 30 feet apart at high altitude.

facts_and_myths.claim: Aerial refueling was invented only recently in the 1990s.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The first aerial refueling took place in 1923 using a simple garden hose between two biplanes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In 1929, the 'Question Mark' aircraft stayed airborne for 150 hours continuously using 43 mid-air refuelings.

name: Turbo-Prop Commuter Plane
visual_anchor: Regional turboprop airliner climbing out over scenic islands with its six-bladed scimitar propellers spinning in the sun.
core_traits: Regional airliner powered by gas turbine engines connected through reduction gearboxes to multi-bladed propellers
Highly fuel-efficient over short regional flight routes between 100 and 500 miles
Operates efficiently on shorter regional runways than pure turbojet passenger airliners
Features pressurized cabins accommodating 30 to 80 passengers for intercity and island hops

facts_and_myths.claim: Turboprop planes use old piston car engines like 1930s aircraft.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Turboprops are true jet turbine engines that use expanding gas to spin a drive shaft rather than relying solely on jet thrust.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Turboprops burn up to 30% less fuel per passenger on short hops compared to regional jets.

facts_and_myths.claim: Turboprop propellers can reverse blade pitch on landing to bring the airplane to a rapid stop without heavy wheel braking.
facts_and_myths.explanation: By shifting propeller blades into negative beta pitch, the propellers blow air forward, acting as powerful airbrakes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Some turboprops can even back up away from an airport gate under their own power using reverse pitch.

name: Space Shuttle
visual_anchor: Iconic black-and-white NASA Space Shuttle orbiter riding a roaring pillar of flame and smoke off Launch Pad 39A.
core_traits: World's first reusable crewed orbital spacecraft system operated by NASA from 1981 to 2011
Launched vertically using two solid rocket boosters and three liquid hydrogen main engines
Orbited Earth at 17,500 mph, deploying satellites, the Hubble Space Telescope, and building the ISS
Reentered Earth atmosphere protected by ceramic thermal tiles and glided to unpowered runway landings

facts_and_myths.claim: The Space Shuttle had jet engines to fly around and circle for a second landing attempt if it missed the runway.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The orbiter was a completely unpowered 100-ton glider during reentry and landing; pilots had exactly one chance to land.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It descended at a steep glide path seven times steeper than a commercial airliner.

facts_and_myths.claim: The black thermal heat tiles on the underside of the shuttle could be held by bare hands immediately after glowing white hot.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Made of 90% air and porous silica ceramic, the tiles dissipate heat so rapidly that their corners can be picked up seconds after exposure to 2,200 degrees.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over 24,000 individually numbered tiles covered each shuttle orbiter.

name: Multi-Stage Rocket
visual_anchor: Mighty skyscraper-sized multi-stage rocket ascending majestically into the twilight sky shedding its first booster stage.
core_traits: Space vehicle utilizing stacked rocket stages to reach orbital velocity or escape Earth gravity
Discards spent propellant tanks and heavy booster engines in sequence as fuel is exhausted to shed dead weight
Propelled by chemical reaction mass combining liquid kerosene or hydrogen with liquid oxygen oxidizer
Pioneered historically by Konstantin Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation and Robert Goddard's liquid rocket tests

facts_and_myths.claim: Rockets push against the air in the atmosphere to propel themselves upward.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Rockets work by Newton's third law of motion (action and reaction), expelling exhaust mass backward; they work even better in the vacuum of space.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Rockets carry their own oxygen oxidizer because there is no air in space.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Apollo Saturn V Moon rocket remains the tallest, heaviest, and most powerful rocket successfully launched for decades.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Standing 363 feet tall and generating 7.5 million pounds of thrust, the Saturn V launched all Apollo Moon landing missions with a 100% success rate.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Saturn V burned 20 tons of rocket fuel every single second at liftoff.

name: International Space Station
visual_anchor: Gigantic International Space Station with glowing gold solar arrays gliding silently against the vivid blue curvature of Earth.
core_traits: Modular habitable artificial satellite orbiting Earth in low Earth orbit at an altitude of 400 kilometers
Continuously occupied by international astronaut crews since November 2000
Spans the size of an entire American football field with pressurized research laboratory modules
Circumnavigates the globe every 90 minutes at a staggering speed of 28,000 km/h (17,500 mph)

facts_and_myths.claim: There is zero gravity on the space station because it is far away from Earth's gravitational pull.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Earth's gravity at ISS altitude is about 90% as strong as on the surface; astronauts float because the station is in permanent freefall around the planet.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Orbiting is simply falling toward the Earth while traveling sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath you.

facts_and_myths.claim: Astronauts aboard the International Space Station witness 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every 24 hours.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because the ISS completes an orbit every 90 minutes, the crew passes between day and night 16 times per Earth day.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Astronauts sleep in small phone-booth-sized sleeping pods tethered in sleeping bags to the wall.

name: Lunar Rover
visual_anchor: Foldable Lunar Roving Vehicle parked near the edge of a deep lunar crater kicking up powdery gray Moon dust in vacuum.
core_traits: Battery-powered electric wheeled vehicle driven by astronauts across the Moon's surface during Apollo 15, 16, and 17
Featured open lawn-chair seating and an aircraft-style T-handle joystick controller
Constructed with lightweight aluminum mesh wheels with titanium chevron treads rather than rubber tires
Folded into a compact origami package tucked into the side quadrant of the Apollo Lunar Module

facts_and_myths.claim: The Apollo Lunar Rovers had inflatable rubber tires like ordinary cars.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Rubber would burst and degrade in the vacuum and extreme lunar temperature swings (-250 to +250 degrees F); wheels were woven zinc-coated piano wire mesh.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The wire mesh acted as natural springs providing excellent traction on soft lunar regolith.

facts_and_myths.claim: All three Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicles remain parked on the surface of the Moon today.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Left behind at the Apollo 15, 16, and 17 landing sites, they still sit undisturbed in the vacuum of space.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Gene Cernan set the unofficial lunar speed record driving one at 11.2 mph (18 km/h).

name: Mars Rover
visual_anchor: Car-sized robotic Mars rover with a high camera mast examining red martian rock layers with its robotic arm drill.
core_traits: Autonomous robotic motorized vehicle designed to explore and traverse the surface of Mars
Equipped with rocker-bogie six-wheel mobility systems to climb over rocks without tipping
Powered by nuclear radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) or solar panel wings
Carries onboard science laboratories, spectrometers, laser rock-vaporizers, and sample collection tubes

facts_and_myths.claim: Engineers at NASA drive Mars rovers in real-time using a video game joystick on Earth.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Radio signals take between 4 and 24 minutes to travel one way between Earth and Mars, making real-time driving impossible.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Rovers navigate autonomously using 3D stereo hazard cameras to plot safe driving paths.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Mars rover Curiosity sang 'Happy Birthday' to itself on the surface of Mars.
facts_and_myths.explanation: On its first anniversary on Mars in August 2013, NASA engineers programmed its sample soil vibration motor to play the tones of the song.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Its aluminum wheels have holes that imprint 'JPL' in Morse code in the martian sand as it drives.

name: Space Telescope
visual_anchor: Gleaming gold hexagonal segmented mirrors of the James Webb Space Telescope floating against the cosmic starfield with its tennis-court sunshield.
core_traits: Astronomical observatory operating in outer space outside the distorting blur and light pollution of Earth's atmosphere
Iconic observatories include the optical Hubble Space Telescope and infrared James Webb Space Telescope
Captures crystal-clear deep-space imagery of distant galaxies, nebulae, exoplanet atmospheres, and stellar nurseries
Operates at extreme distances such as low Earth orbit or the gravitationally stable Sun-Earth Lagrange Point 2

facts_and_myths.claim: The James Webb Space Telescope orbits Earth inside low Earth orbit right next to Hubble.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hubble orbits 340 miles above Earth, but Webb is located 1 million miles away at Lagrange Point 2 where astronauts cannot reach it.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Webb operates at nearly absolute zero (-390 degrees F) protected by a 5-layer tennis-court-sized sunshield.

facts_and_myths.claim: Space telescopes act as time machines, observing galaxies as they existed over 13 billion years ago.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because light takes billions of years to travel across the cosmos, telescopes see the most distant objects as they looked when the universe was young.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Webb's beryllium primary mirror is coated in an ultra-thin layer of real vaporized gold just 100 nanometers thick.

name: Communications Satellite
visual_anchor: Modern communications satellite in geostationary orbit with gleaming blue solar panels unfurled above the glowing blue Earth.
core_traits: Artificial satellite placed in orbit around Earth to relay telecommunications, television, internet, and data signals
Equipped with transponders that receive radio signals from Earth ground stations, amplify them, and beam them back down
Many operate in Geostationary Orbit (GEO) at 35,786 kilometers, appearing fixed over a single spot on the equator
Powered by large solar array wings and stabilized by reaction wheels and ion thruster station-keeping

facts_and_myths.claim: Science fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke invented the concept of geostationary communications satellites in 1945.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Clarke published a landmark paper proposing three orbital relay stations at 36,000 km altitude to provide worldwide radio coverage.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The geostationary orbit band is frequently honored as the 'Clarke Orbit' in recognition of his vision.

facts_and_myths.claim: All communications satellites stay in orbit forever without needing any steering or propulsion.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Gravitational tugs from the Moon, Sun, and Earth oblateness require satellites to use station-keeping thrusters to maintain position.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: At the end of their 15-year operational lives, geostationary satellites are boosted into a graveyard orbit higher up.

name: Apollo Lunar Module
visual_anchor: Gold-foil wrapped Apollo Lunar Module standing on four spindly footpads on the desolate gray moonscape.
core_traits: Two-stage crewed spacecraft that landed Apollo astronauts on the Moon between 1969 and 1972
Consisted of a descent stage with landing legs and an ascent stage with crew cabin and rocket engine
World's first true crewed spacecraft designed to operate exclusively in the vacuum of space
Allowed Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to achieve the historic Apollo 11 lunar landing

facts_and_myths.claim: The skin of the Apollo Lunar Module was so thin that an astronaut could poke a pencil through it.
facts_and_myths.explanation: To save crucial weight, parts of the pressurized aluminum hull were just 0.012 inches (0.3 mm) thick, about three layers of kitchen foil.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Because there was no air resistance or weather on the Moon, aerodynamic design was completely unnecessary.

facts_and_myths.claim: Astronauts had comfortable chairs to sit in while landing the Lunar Module on the Moon.
facts_and_myths.explanation: There were no chairs inside the cabin; astronauts stood upright during landing and takeoff, held by bungee cables to save weight.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Standing gave astronauts better visibility through the small triangular landing windows.

name: Space Capsule
visual_anchor: Scorched blunt-body space capsule deploying three huge orange-and-white parachutes as it descends toward ocean splashdown.
core_traits: Blunt-body spacecraft design used to launch and return astronauts safely through Earth's atmosphere
Features a conical or gumdrop aerodynamic shape with a curved heat shield on the bottom base
Uses ablative heat shields to withstand 3,000-degree atmospheric reentry temperatures
Lands on Earth via multi-stage parachutes splashing down in water or touching down on land with cushioning thrusters

facts_and_myths.claim: Space capsules have wings to steer and fly around airports like an airplane.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Space capsules are wingless craft that follow a ballistic or lifting-body trajectory, relying entirely on parachutes to land.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Capsules use small thrusters to roll and tilt slightly to control their atmospheric entry corridor.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Russian Soyuz space capsule has been in continuous operational service for over 50 years.
facts_and_myths.explanation: First flying in 1967, iteratively modernized variants of Soyuz have completed hundreds of crewed flights to Salyut, Mir, and the ISS.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It is widely regarded as one of the most reliable human spacecraft ever built.

name: Interplanetary Space Probe
visual_anchor: Solitary golden-dish Voyager robotic space probe sailing silently past the banded rings of Saturn into deep cosmic darkness.
core_traits: Uncrewed robotic spacecraft launched to explore distant planets, moons, asteroids, and outer reaches of the solar system
Powered by nuclear radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) when traveling far from solar sunlight
Equipped with large high-gain dish antennas to transmit scientific sensor data across billions of miles of space
Exemplified by Voyager 1 and 2, which launched in 1977 and became the first human-made objects in interstellar space

facts_and_myths.claim: Voyager 1 and 2 carry a Golden Record containing sounds, music, and images of Earth for extraterrestrial life.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Curated by Carl Sagan, the 12-inch gold-plated copper phonograph records carry greetings in 55 languages and nature sounds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The records come with visual instructions and a stylus explaining how to play them.

facts_and_myths.claim: Space probes use up all their rocket fuel continuously while traveling between planets.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In the friction-free vacuum of space, probes coast for years on inertia after initial propulsion and use planetary gravity assists.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A gravity assist slingshot steals a tiny fraction of a planet's orbital momentum to accelerate the probe.

name: Solar Observatory Satellite
visual_anchor: Heavily shielded solar probe diving close to the blinding fiery corona of the Sun with dynamic solar flares arching outward.
core_traits: Scientific spacecraft designed specifically to observe the Sun, solar wind, coronal mass ejections, and space weather
Carries specialized ultraviolet and X-ray telescopes, magnetometers, and solar energetic particle detectors
Equipped with thick carbon-composite heat shields to survive blistering temperatures thousands of degrees hot
NASA's Parker Solar Probe became the first spacecraft to officially 'touch the Sun' by flying through its outer corona

facts_and_myths.claim: Parker Solar Probe is the fastest human-made object ever constructed in history.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Using Venus gravity assists, the probe reaches peak orbital speeds exceeding 430,000 mph (700,000 km/h) around the Sun.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: At top speed, it could travel from New York to Tokyo in less than one minute.

facts_and_myths.claim: The scientific instruments on a solar probe melt instantly when approaching the Sun.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A 4.5-inch-thick carbon-composite thermal shield keeps instruments behind it safely operating at a comfortable room temperature (about 85 degrees F).
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Autonomous sensors on the probe immediately correct its orientation if even a tiny sliver of sunlight peeks past the shield.

name: Reusable Rocket Booster
visual_anchor: Tall soot-stained rocket first stage firing its center landing engine and deploying four grid fins to touch down gently on an ocean drone ship.
core_traits: Orbital rocket stage engineered to return to Earth, land vertically, and be refurbished for multiple space launches
Uses hypersonic titanium grid fins to steer aerodynamically back down through the upper atmosphere
Performs precision boostback, entry, and landing burns using liquid propellant rocket engines
Pioneered commercially by SpaceX's Falcon 9, drastically slashing the cost of accessing Earth orbit

facts_and_myths.claim: Before 2015, all orbital rocket first stages were completely discarded and lost in the ocean after every single flight.
facts_and_myths.explanation: For over 50 years of spaceflight, million-dollar rocket boosters were treated as single-use disposable hardware.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Landing and reusing boosters has reduced launch costs by over 70%.

facts_and_myths.claim: Reusable rocket boosters use parachutes to float down slowly onto their ocean landing platforms.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Boosters land propulsively, using pinpoint rocket engine thrust to decelerate from supersonic speeds to zero velocity at touchdown.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The maneuver is known as a 'hoverslam' or 'suicide burn' because the rocket cannot hover; it must reach zero speed precisely at ground level.

name: Astronaut Jetpack
visual_anchor: Astronaut floating untethered in the profound black void of space above Earth wearing a white thruster backpack.
core_traits: Propulsion backpack device that allows astronauts to perform untethered spacewalks (EVAs) outside a spacecraft
