Equipped with 24 high-pressure gaseous nitrogen thrusters distributed around the unit for 6 degrees of freedom
Controlled via hand controllers mounted on armrests to provide pinpoint translation and rotation in zero gravity
Famously tested by astronaut Bruce McCandless II in 1984 during Space Shuttle mission STS-41-B

facts_and_myths.claim: Bruce McCandless floated more than 300 feet away from the Space Shuttle with zero safety tether connecting him.
facts_and_myths.explanation: His historic untethered spacewalk in 1984 produced one of the most famous and harrowing photographs in human history.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: McCandless later stated that the quietest and most peaceful moment of his life was floating alone in the void.

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern spacewalkers use full-sized MMU jetpacks on every routine space station maintenance walk.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The large MMU was retired; modern astronauts use tethers and carry a compact emergency nitrogen pack called SAFER just in case a tether snaps.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: SAFER has only enough propellant to return an astronaut to the station structure if accidentally detached.

name: Lunar Lander
visual_anchor: Multilateral robotic lunar lander with gleaming gold thermal foil sitting quietly on the rugged rim of the lunar South Pole.
core_traits: Spacecraft designed to descend from lunar orbit and execute a controlled soft landing on the surface of the Moon
Equipped with throttleable descent rocket engines and laser terrain-relative navigation LIDAR sensors
Deploys robotic rovers, scientific seismometers, and drill payloads to analyze lunar soil and water ice
Features shock-absorbing landing legs designed to prevent tipping on uneven boulders or crater slopes

facts_and_myths.claim: Landing on the Moon is easier than landing on Mars because the Moon has no atmosphere to burn up the craft.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Having no atmosphere means parachutes are completely useless; 100% of deceleration must be performed by firing rocket engines.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Spacecraft must shed over 3,600 mph of orbital velocity entirely with rocket propellant to touch down gently.

facts_and_myths.claim: India's Chandrayaan-3 mission made history in 2023 by landing near the Moon's unexplored South Pole.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Vikram lander successfully touched down near the southern polar region where permanently shadowed craters contain water ice.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Lunar water ice can be processed into liquid hydrogen and oxygen rocket propellant for deep space exploration.

name: Mars Helicopter
visual_anchor: Compact carbon-fiber dual-rotor Mars helicopter hovering ten meters above red dusty sands with rocky Martian hills in the backdrop.
core_traits: Autonomous robotic coaxial rotorcraft designed to test powered, controlled flight in the thin atmosphere of Mars
Features counter-rotating carbon-composite rotor blades spinning at an astonishing 2,400 to 2,700 RPM
Powered by a small solar panel charging lithium-ion batteries with internal heating elements to survive freezing Martian nights
Achieved historic first powered controlled flight on another planet in April 2021 as NASA's Ingenuity

facts_and_myths.claim: Flying a helicopter on Mars is easy because gravity is only one-third of Earth's gravity.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mars' atmosphere is less than 1% as dense as Earth's, equivalent to flying at 100,000 feet altitude on Earth, requiring extreme rotor speeds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ingenuity's blades spin five to six times faster than typical helicopter blades on Earth.

facts_and_myths.claim: NASA's Ingenuity was originally designed for only 5 short test flights, but completed over 70 successful flights.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Expected to last just 30 days, Ingenuity operated for nearly three years serving as an aerial scout for the Perseverance rover.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It carried a tiny postage-stamp-sized piece of fabric from the Wright brothers' 1903 Flyer wing underneath its solar panel.

name: Cargo Resupply Spacecraft
visual_anchor: Robotic automated cargo capsule executing precision proximity docking with the International Space Station docking port.
core_traits: Uncrewed automated spacecraft engineered to deliver food, water, spare parts, and science experiments to orbiting space stations
Navigates autonomously in space using star trackers, optical LIDAR, and GPS relative navigation
Either docks directly with the station or is captured by the station's robotic arm (Canadarm2)
Some variants (like Dragon) return scientific cargo safely to Earth, while others burn up harmlessly in the atmosphere carrying trash

facts_and_myths.claim: Astronauts aboard the space station use expendable cargo spacecraft as giant flying garbage disposals.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Uncrewed Russian Progress and Northrop Grumman Cygnus ships are filled with station waste and intentionally incinerated during atmospheric reentry.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The cargo ship and tons of trash burn up completely into shooting stars over the uninhabited South Pacific ocean.

facts_and_myths.claim: Cargo resupply ships must be manually steered into the docking hatch by astronauts using joysticks.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern cargo vessels like SpaceX's Cargo Dragon dock fully autonomously using onboard guidance computers without human intervention.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Astronauts monitor the approach with an emergency abort button if the spacecraft strays outside its safe approach cone.

name: Weather Satellite
visual_anchor: High-tech meteorological satellite tracking the swirling white spiral eye of a colossal Category 5 hurricane over the blue ocean.
core_traits: Earth-observing artificial satellite primarily used to monitor the weather, climate, and storm systems across the globe
Operates in either geostationary orbits for constant regional surveillance or polar orbits for high-resolution global scans
Equipped with visible, infrared, and microwave radiometers to measure cloud cover, ocean temperatures, and atmospheric moisture
Provides critical early warning detection for hurricanes, typhoons, severe thunderstorms, and wildfires

facts_and_myths.claim: Weather satellites can only take photographs during broad daylight when the sun is shining.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Infrared and microwave sensors detect heat radiation emitted by clouds and Earth's surface, tracking storms 24/7 in complete darkness.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Thermal imaging allows meteorologists to determine the precise height and strength of storm clouds based on cloud-top temperatures.

facts_and_myths.claim: The world's first successful weather satellite was TIROS-1, launched in 1960.
facts_and_myths.explanation: TIROS-1 returned the first television pictures of Earth's cloud patterns from space, revolutionizing global meteorology forever.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Before weather satellites, massive ocean hurricanes could strike coastlines with almost zero advance warning.

name: GPS Navigation Satellite
visual_anchor: Solar-paneled navigation satellite broadcasting precision timing radio waves down to Earth while orbiting in medium Earth orbit.
core_traits: Satellite forming part of a global constellation broadcasting ultra-precise radio timing signals to determine user location
Operates in medium Earth orbit at an altitude of approximately 20,200 kilometers
Carries atomic clocks (rubidium and cesium) accurate to within a few billionths of a second per day
Enables worldwide positioning, turn-by-turn vehicle navigation, aviation routing, and global financial timestamp synchronization

facts_and_myths.claim: Your smartphone sends a radio signal up to GPS satellites so the satellites can track your location.
facts_and_myths.explanation: GPS is purely one-way broadcast; satellites constantly transmit time signals, and your device simply listens and calculates position.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Because your phone only receives, millions of people can use GPS simultaneously without overloading the satellites.

facts_and_myths.claim: GPS satellites must account for Einstein's theories of Special and General Relativity to maintain accuracy.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Due to high orbital velocity and weaker gravity, satellite atomic clocks tick 38 microseconds faster per day than clocks on Earth.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Without relativistic mathematical corrections, GPS location calculations would drift by over 10 kilometers every single day.

name: Orbital Space Laboratory
visual_anchor: Modular orbital space laboratory with expansive solar wings and docked science experiment modules orbiting above the aurora borealis.
core_traits: Inhabited orbital research station dedicated to conducting microgravity experiments in physics, biology, and materials science
Pioneered by early stations such as the Soviet Salyut program, America's Skylab, and Russia's modular Mir station
Equipped with gloveboxes, centrifuges, plant-growth chambers, and external exposed experiment platforms
Studies how long-duration spaceflight affects the human cardiovascular, muscular, and immune systems

facts_and_myths.claim: Skylab was constructed inside the hollowed-out upper third stage of a massive Saturn V rocket.
facts_and_myths.explanation: NASA converted the empty hydrogen fuel tank of an S-IVB rocket stage into a two-story orbital living space and laboratory in 1973.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Skylab had so much open interior volume that astronauts could literally run around a circular track on its inner walls.

facts_and_myths.claim: Fire behaves the same way in an orbital space lab as it does on Earth.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Without gravity-driven buoyancy convection, warm air does not rise; flames in zero gravity burn as dim, spherical blue fireballs.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Flames produce very little soot in microgravity because oxygen diffuses slowly toward the center from all directions.

name: CubeSat
visual_anchor: Tiny 10-centimeter cube satellite deploying its miniature solar panels and spring-loaded antennas into Earth orbit from a deployer tube.
core_traits: Miniaturized artificial satellite built with standardized cubic units of 10x10x10 cm dimensions (known as 1U)
Weighs between 1 and 10 kilograms, drastically democratizing access to space for universities and small startups
Utilizes commercial off-the-shelf electronic components, micro-thrusters, and miniature imaging sensors
Launched as secondary hitchhiker payloads on commercial rockets or released from the ISS deployer

facts_and_myths.claim: CubeSats are merely student classroom toys incapable of deep space exploration.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 2018, NASA's twin MarCO CubeSats flew all the way to Mars, successfully relaying real-time landing telemetry from the InSight lander.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The MarCO CubeSats used compressed cold-gas thrusters powered by ordinary fire extinguisher propellant.

facts_and_myths.claim: Standard CubeSat dimensions were created in 1999 by professors at Stanford and Cal Poly.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Jordi Puig-Suari and Bob Twiggs created the standard so graduate students could design, build, and launch a satellite within a degree cycle.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over 2,000 CubeSats have been successfully launched into space to date.

name: Deep Space Probe
visual_anchor: Cassini spacecraft firing its main braking engine to slip into orbit around the golden glowing cloud bands of Saturn.
core_traits: Heavy robotic exploration craft launched to conduct multi-year in-depth orbital tours of outer planets and their moons
Exemplified by flagship missions like Galileo at Jupiter and Cassini at Saturn
Carried deployable landing probes, such as the European Huygens probe that descended onto Saturn's giant moon Titan
Revolutionized planetary science by discovering subsurface oceans on icy moons like Enceladus and Europa

facts_and_myths.claim: The Cassini probe discovered active geysers of liquid water blasting into space from Saturn's tiny moon Enceladus.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Cassini flew directly through the icy plume spray, tasting water vapor, salts, and organic molecules erupting from a warm subsurface ocean.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Enceladus' icy geysers actually create and replenish Saturn's entire diffuse E ring.

facts_and_myths.claim: When Cassini ran out of fuel, NASA left it to drift around Saturn as permanent space junk.
facts_and_myths.explanation: NASA intentionally crashed Cassini into Saturn's crushing atmosphere in 2017 to eliminate any risk of contaminating pristine moons with Earth microbes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: This dramatic fiery dive into Saturn's atmosphere was known as the 'Grand Finale'.

name: Sample Return Capsule
visual_anchor: Charred aerodynamic sample return capsule resting safely on the cracked desert flats of Utah after landing from deep space.
core_traits: Specialized spacecraft reentry vessel designed to carry pristine physical rock, dust, or soil samples collected from other celestial bodies back to Earth
Equipped with thick ablative heat shields engineered to survive violent hyperbolic reentry speeds exceeding 27,000 mph
Features hermetically sealed robotic sample canisters to preserve extraterrestrial material from Earth atmosphere contamination
Successfully returned samples from comets, the Moon, and asteroids such as Ryugu and Bennu

facts_and_myths.claim: NASA's OSIRIS-REx spacecraft returned over 120 grams of pristine asteroid rubble from asteroid Bennu in 2023.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The mission gathered dark carbon-rich gravel and dust from Bennu, delivering the largest asteroid sample ever brought to Earth.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Scientists found water-bearing minerals and organic carbon molecules dating back to the dawn of the solar system.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sample return capsules require human astronauts on board to operate the landing parachute release.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They are completely autonomous robotic capsules that trigger drogue and main parachutes via barometric and acceleration sensors.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Recovery teams rush to the capsule with mobile cleanrooms to prevent even a single grain of Earth dust from touching the sample.

name: Crew Spacecraft
visual_anchor: Sleek futuristic crew spacecraft with illuminated white touchscreens and four astronauts seated in molded black carbon seats.
core_traits: Modern human-rated spacecraft designed to ferry astronauts to the International Space Station and beyond to the Moon
Equipped with integrated launch escape thrusters capable of pulling the crew away from a failing rocket in a fraction of a second
Features modern minimalist glass cockpits operated primarily via large digital capacitive touchscreens
Capable of autonomous rendezvous, orbital docking, atmospheric reentry, and precision parachute recovery

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern crew spacecraft like SpaceX Crew Dragon use mechanical switches and analog dials like the Apollo capsules.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Crew Dragon cockpits use three large custom touchscreen displays with glove-compatible capacitive touch; mechanical buttons are minimal backups.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Astronauts wear custom-tailored pressurized flight suits with touchscreen-conductive fingertips.

facts_and_myths.claim: Launch escape systems can accelerate a crew spacecraft from zero to 100 mph in just over one second.
facts_and_myths.explanation: High-thrust SuperDraco engines generate instantaneous thrust to pull the crew capsule safely away from an exploding rocket.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The escape system functions reliably anywhere from the launch pad all the way into space.

name: Solar Sail Spacecraft
visual_anchor: Dazzling mirror-reflective aluminized Mylar solar sail stretching dozens of meters wide shimmering in cosmic sunlight.
core_traits: Spacecraft propelled entirely by the radiation pressure of sunlight bouncing off gigantic ultra-thin reflective sails
Requires zero onboard chemical rocket propellant to accelerate continuously across interplanetary space
Constructed from micro-thin aluminized Kapton or Mylar films only a fraction of the thickness of a human hair
Demonstrated successfully in space by Japan's IKAROS in 2010 and The Planetary Society's LightSail 2 in 2019

facts_and_myths.claim: Solar sails are pushed through space by the solar wind of blowing gas particles.
facts_and_myths.explanation: While solar wind particles exist, 99% of a solar sail's thrust comes from the pure momentum transfer of bouncing light photons.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Although photons have no rest mass, they carry kinetic momentum that exerts real physical pressure on reflective surfaces.

facts_and_myths.claim: A solar sail can theoretically accelerate indefinitely as long as sunlight strikes its reflective surface.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Without consuming chemical fuel, constant solar photon pressure provides endless acceleration, eventually reaching incredible interstellar speeds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Science concepts like Breakthrough Starshot propose using powerful ground lasers to push micro-sails to 20% the speed of light.

name: Bullet Train
visual_anchor: Aerodynamic long-nosed Japanese Shinkansen bullet train streaking past snow-capped Mount Fuji at 320 km/h.
core_traits: Pioneering network of high-speed passenger rail trains introduced in Japan in 1964 with the Tokaido Shinkansen
Features needle-nosed aerodynamic front ends designed to eliminate tunnel sonic booms
Operates on dedicated standard-gauge continuously welded rail tracks with no level grade crossings
Renowned globally for near-flawless punctuality measured in mere seconds of average annual delay

facts_and_myths.claim: The long, duck-billed nose of the 500-series Shinkansen train was inspired by the beak of a kingfisher bird.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Engineers studied how the kingfisher dives silently from air into dense water, shaping the nose to stop violent tunnel pressure waves.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The biomimetic design also reduced electricity consumption by 15% and increased speed by 10%.

facts_and_myths.claim: In its 60-year history carrying over 10 billion passengers, zero passengers have died from Shinkansen train collisions or derailments.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Strict automatic train control (ATC) systems and automatic earthquake emergency braking have maintained a legendary safety record.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: During major earthquakes, onboard sensors cut power and apply emergency brakes seconds before the seismic shaking arrives.

name: Monorail
visual_anchor: Sleek futuristic white monorail gliding silently on an elevated concrete guidebeam through a lush urban theme park.
core_traits: Railway system in which the track consists of a single concrete or steel guidebeam
Trains either straddle the top of the narrow beam or hang suspended from an overhead monorail track
Utilizes rubber drive tires running along the top and side of the beam for whisper-quiet electric propulsion
Commonly deployed in theme parks, international airports, and dense metropolitan transit corridors

facts_and_myths.claim: Monorail tracks are much easier and cheaper to switch between tracks than conventional two-rail train tracks.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Switching tracks requires mechanically moving an entire massive multi-ton concrete beam segment, which is complex and slow.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: This track-switching complexity is why monorails are rarely used for complex mainline rail networks.

facts_and_myths.claim: Germany's Wuppertal Schwebebahn is a historic suspended monorail that has operated continuously since 1901.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The train hangs suspended from an elevated steel frame over the Wupper river, moving tens of thousands of daily commuters.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In 1950, a young circus elephant named Tuffi jumped out of the suspended monorail into the river below and survived.

name: Maglev Train
visual_anchor: Ultra-modern maglev train hovering frictionlessly inches above its guideway levitation magnets cruising at 500 km/h.
core_traits: Train transportation system that uses magnetic levitation to lift, guide, and propel train cars with zero physical track contact
Eliminates rolling wheel friction, mechanical wear, and track vibration entirely
Propelled along the guideway by linear induction or synchronous electric motors embedded in the tracks
Holds the world railway speed record at 603 km/h (375 mph) set by Japan's L0 Series SCMaglev

facts_and_myths.claim: Maglev trains have steel wheels that roll along rails at high speeds.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Maglev trains have no wheels on the track at speed; they float on a magnetic cushion roughly 1 to 10 centimeters above the guidepath.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Because there is no track friction, the only significant drag comes from air resistance.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Shanghai Maglev is the world's fastest commercial operating train in regular public service.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Connecting Pudong Airport to Shanghai, it cruises at up to 431 km/h (268 mph), completing the 30-km trip in about 7 minutes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Its powerful electromagnetic fields are so well shielded that they emit less magnetic interference than a household hairdryer.

name: Subway
visual_anchor: Stainless steel subway train pulling into an illuminated subterranean tiled underground station packed with commuters.
core_traits: Underground urban rapid transit electric railway system operating on dedicated subterranean tracks
Powered by electrified third rails or overhead catenary wire systems delivering high-voltage current
Transports hundreds of thousands of urban passengers daily completely separated from street traffic congestion
Iconic world systems include the London Underground, New York City Subway, Tokyo Metro, and Paris Metro

facts_and_myths.claim: The London Underground, opened in 1863, originally operated using smoke-billowing steam engines underground.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Early underground lines used coal-fired steam locomotives with condensing pipes before electric traction was adopted in 1890.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Stations had to be built with open blowholes and vents to let suffocating coal smoke escape to street level.

facts_and_myths.claim: Subway trains generate all their electricity from their own diesel engines on board.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Subways are 100% electric, drawing power from external electrified third rails running alongside the running tracks.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The New York City subway system operates 24 hours a day, 365 days a year across 472 stations.

name: Cable Car
visual_anchor: Historic wooden San Francisco cable car climbing a dizzyingly steep hill with passengers gripping external running boards.
core_traits: Historic street railway vehicle propelled by latching onto a continuously moving steel cable beneath the street slot
Operated by a gripman who uses a mechanical clamping lever to grab or release the moving underground cable
Has zero motor or engine inside the car itself; all propulsion power comes from a central stationary powerhouse
Conquers extraordinarily steep urban hills that ordinary wheeled steel trains or early horse carriages could never climb

facts_and_myths.claim: Cable cars have an engine or electric battery inside the vehicle to turn the wheels.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The cars are completely unpowered; they move solely by physically clamping onto a continuous 9.5 mph underground steel wire.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: When stopping, the gripman releases the clamp and applies wooden brake blocks directly against the steel rails.

facts_and_myths.claim: The San Francisco cable car system is the world's last manually operated permanent cable car railway.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Designated a US National Historic Landmark, it has operated continuously since Andrew Hallidie invented it in 1873.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Hallidie was inspired after seeing horses slip and die trying to pull heavy wagons up wet cobbled hills.

name: Tram
visual_anchor: Modern low-floor yellow electric tram gliding gracefully down a pedestrianized European boulevard alongside cyclists.
core_traits: Passenger rail vehicle that runs on grooved tracks laid flush into public urban street pavement
Powered by electricity drawn from overhead wires via a rooftop pantograph or trolley pole
Shares roadway corridors with pedestrians, bicycles, and general vehicular road traffic
Provides accessible, frequent, zero-emission urban transit in hundreds of cities worldwide

facts_and_myths.claim: Trams and subways run on the exact same kind of tracks with dangerous exposed third rails in the street.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Trams draw electricity from safe overhead catenary wires; an electrified third rail in a public street would electrocute pedestrians.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Some modern trams use ground-level induction power that only activates when covered by the train body.

facts_and_myths.claim: Melbourne, Australia operates the largest urban tram network in the world.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The network spans 250 kilometers of track, operating nearly 500 trams over 24 routes across the metropolitan area.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Melbourne's City Circle heritage tram route operates completely free of charge for tourists and residents.

name: Diesel Locomotive
visual_anchor: Massive roaring 4,400-horsepower yellow diesel-electric locomotive leading a two-mile-long freight train through desert canyons.
core_traits: Railway locomotive powered by a massive multi-cylinder diesel engine coupled to an electric generator
Operates as a mobile diesel-electric power station driving heavy electric traction motors on the wheel axles
Gradually replaced steam locomotives across the globe in the mid-20th century due to vastly superior efficiency and reliability
Forms the heavy backbone of freight rail haulage across North America, Australia, and non-electrified worldwide routes

facts_and_myths.claim: A diesel locomotive engine directly turns the train wheels through a mechanical clutch and transmission like a manual car.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Virtually all modern diesel locomotives are diesel-electric; the diesel engine spins an alternator to generate electricity for electric axle motors.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A mechanical clutch could never handle the brutal torque required to start a 10,000-ton train moving.

facts_and_myths.claim: Freight trains pulled by diesel-electric locomotives can move one ton of freight nearly 500 miles on a single gallon of fuel.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Steel wheels rolling on steel rails produce minimal friction, making freight rail four times more fuel-efficient than trucking.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Locomotive engines have displacements exceeding 180 liters with cylinders the size of paint buckets.

name: High-Speed Electric Train
visual_anchor: Sharp silver and blue French TGV train streaking across a scenic viaduct through sunflower fields at 300 km/h.
core_traits: Modern electric passenger train engineered for sustained commercial cruising speeds of 250 to 350 km/h (155 to 217 mph)
Powered by overhead catenary lines supplying 25,000 volts of high-voltage alternating current
Features articulated car bogies and lightweight aluminum/composite aerodynamic styling
Iconic European systems include France's TGV, Germany's ICE, and Italy's Frecciarossa

facts_and_myths.claim: A French TGV holds the world record for the fastest speed ever achieved by a conventional wheeled rail train.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In April 2007, a specially modified TGV V150 reached a mind-boggling 574.8 km/h (357.2 mph) on steel rails.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The electrical catenary wire had to be heavily tensioned to prevent the pantograph from outrunning the electrical wave.

facts_and_myths.claim: High-speed electric trains cause severe air pollution in cities because they run on electricity.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Electric trains produce zero direct emissions along their travel corridor and generate up to 90% fewer carbon emissions per passenger than flying.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: High-speed rail has largely replaced short-haul domestic flights across France, Spain, and Germany.

name: Freight Train
visual_anchor: Miles-long freight train snaking through winding mountain passes stacked two-high with colorful intermodal shipping containers.
core_traits: Group of connected rail cars hauled by one or more locomotives to transport heavy goods, bulk materials, or containers
Often exceeds one to two miles in total length, pulling thousands of tons of cargo
Equipped with automatic air brake systems running the length of the train to provide synchronized stopping power
Hauls coal, grain, chemicals, manufactured automobiles, and intermodal shipping containers worldwide

facts_and_myths.claim: A fully loaded two-mile freight train traveling at 55 mph can take over a mile to come to a complete stop.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Due to enormous kinetic mass and low steel-on-steel friction, emergency stopping distance can equal 18 football fields.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A train hitting an automobile has the same physical force ratio as a car running over a soda can.

facts_and_myths.claim: Freight trains in the US can stack shipping containers two-high on top of each other.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Double-stack container trains use depressed well cars to keep the overall height low enough to clear bridges and tunnels.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Double stacking nearly doubled container rail capacity overnight when introduced in the 1980s.

name: Cog Railway
visual_anchor: Stout red cog railway train climbing an impossibly steep 48-degree gradient up the sheer rocky face of Mount Pilatus in Switzerland.
core_traits: Steep grade railway utilizing a toothed center rack rail positioned between running rails engaged by drive cog wheels
Overcomes the physical traction limits of standard steel wheels which slip on slopes steeper than 7%
Engineered to scale towering mountain peaks in the Swiss Alps, Rocky Mountains, and Andes
Features redundant emergency ratchet and dynamic clamp brakes to prevent catastrophic runaway rollbacks

facts_and_myths.claim: The Pilatus Railway in Switzerland is the steepest cogwheel railway in the world.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It features a maximum gradient of 48% and uses a unique horizontal Locher rack system to prevent the cogs from jumping out.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The train cars are built with stepped, tiered passenger compartments to keep passengers level on the incline.

facts_and_myths.claim: Cog railways rely purely on friction between normal train wheels and rails to climb mountains.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They rely directly on mechanical gear teeth intermeshing with a central steel rack bar; friction alone would cause wheels to spin uselessly.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Mount Washington Cog Railway in New Hampshire was the world's first mountain rack railway, built in 1869.

name: Commuter Train
visual_anchor: Silver multi-level commuter passenger train speeding alongside a congested highway gridlock at morning rush hour.
core_traits: Passenger train service operating between central metropolitan hubs and surrounding suburban commuter communities
Features frequent schedules aligned with morning and evening business commuting peaks
Typically uses double-decker gallery passenger coaches or electric multiple units with wide doors for rapid passenger flow
Operates push-pull configurations with a cab control car at one end and a locomotive at the other

facts_and_myths.claim: Push-pull commuter trains must turn the entire locomotive around on a turntable at the end of every trip.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The train operates in reverse without turning; the engineer controls the rear locomotive remotely from a cab car at the front.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Push-pull operation eliminates the time-consuming need to switch or decouple locomotives at terminal stations.

facts_and_myths.claim: Commuter trains are the same thing as urban subway systems.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Commuter rail covers much longer distances (20 to 60 miles) with larger stations and operates to a scheduled timetable rather than subway headway frequency.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Commuter trains often share mainline tracks with heavy national freight trains.

name: Elevated Train
visual_anchor: Iconic steel Chicago 'L' train rumbling across elevated rivet-studded iron trestles high above bustling downtown city traffic.
core_traits: Rapid transit railway with tracks built on an elevated steel, iron, or concrete viaduct structure above street level
Eliminates collisions with pedestrians and automobiles by separating grade levels without expensive deep tunneling
World-famous systems include the Chicago 'L', New York's historic elevated lines, and Vancouver's automated SkyTrain
Brings natural daylight and scenic skyline views to urban transit passengers

facts_and_myths.claim: The famous Chicago 'L' rapid transit system is named after the word 'Loop'.
facts_and_myths.explanation: 'L' is simply short for 'elevated'; the downtown historic track circuit was named 'The Loop' because the tracks form a literal elevated rectangle.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Chicago's elevated trains first began operating with steam engines in 1892 before converting to electricity.

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern elevated automated systems like Vancouver's SkyTrain operate without a human driver aboard.
facts_and_myths.explanation: SkyTrain uses moving-block computerized automatic train control to govern acceleration, braking, and door operations safely.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It is one of the longest fully automated driverless rapid transit systems in the world.

name: Handcar
visual_anchor: Two railway workers rhythmically pumping a walking-beam seesaw handle to propel a vintage wooden handcar down the tracks.
core_traits: Small railroad car powered by passengers pumping a seesaw walking-beam lever up and down
Used historically by railroad track inspection crews and maintenance gangs to inspect remote track lines
Mechanical gears connect the hand pump to the wheel axles to translate human muscle power into forward motion
Iconic fixture of classic Western cinema and early railway lore before gasoline speeders replaced them

facts_and_myths.claim: Handcars could reach speeds of over 20 miles per hour if two strong workers pumped rapidly.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Geared drive mechanisms allowed a pair of coordinated trackmen to propel the lightweight wooden car surprisingly fast on flat rails.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Annual handcar races are still held as heritage sports events in historic railroad towns.

facts_and_myths.claim: Handcars had heavy cowcatchers and steam whistles to clear animals from the tracks.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Handcars were minimalist open wooden platforms weighing only a few hundred pounds; crews relied on foot brakes and loud yelling.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: If a real train appeared, the crew's only option was to quickly lift the handcar off the rails into the ditch.

name: Intercity Passenger Train
visual_anchor: Sleek diesel-electric passenger train cruising through the scenic Pacific Northwest coastline alongside crashing ocean waves.
core_traits: Long-distance passenger train connecting major cities across regions or countries
Features comfortable reclining coach seats, cafe cars, dining cars, and panoramic observation lounge cars
Operates at higher speeds with fewer station stops than local or commuter rail services
Serves as a comfortable, scenic alternative to highway driving and regional domestic air travel

facts_and_myths.claim: Intercity passenger trains in North America own all their own tracks and always have right-of-way over freight trains.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Outside the Northeast Corridor, passenger trains like Amtrak operate largely on tracks owned by commercial freight railroads, often causing dispatch delays.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Federal law technically grants passenger trains preference, but freight rail congestion frequently causes side-tracking.

facts_and_myths.claim: Many long-distance passenger trains offer full-service dining cars where chefs prepare hot meals in an onboard galley kitchen.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Transcontinental trains feature full commercial kitchens preparing steaks, seafood, and fresh breakfasts served on linen-covered tables.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Glass-domed observation cars allow passengers 360-degree views of mountain ranges and river canyons.

name: Double-Decker Train
visual_anchor: Massive silver two-story passenger train standing tall beside a suburban platform with passengers boarding upper and lower decks.
core_traits: Passenger train car featuring two levels of passenger seating, connected by interior stairs
Increases passenger carrying capacity by up to 50% to 70% without lengthening the train or platforms
Common on busy suburban commuter routes and long-distance trains with generous overhead clearances
Exemplified by French TGV Duplex high-speed trains and American Amtrak Superliner coaches

facts_and_myths.claim: High-speed 300 km/h trains cannot be double-deckers because they would be top-heavy and tip over.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The French TGV Duplex is an articulated double-decker train that cruises safely at 320 km/h and holds over 500 passengers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Its low center of gravity is maintained by placing heavy transformers and motors low on the chassis.

facts_and_myths.claim: Double-decker trains cannot operate in Britain because historic Victorian bridges and tunnels are too low.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Britain's restrictive railway 'loading gauge' built in the 1800s prevents full-height double-decker passenger trains from clearing bridges.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: North America has a very tall loading gauge, permitting massive two-story passenger and double-stack container trains.

name: Luxury Sleeper Train
visual_anchor: Lavishly appointed dark blue and gold vintage sleeper train with polished mahogany compartments and glowing brass reading lamps.
core_traits: Overnight passenger train providing private sleeping cabins, dining carriages, and luxury hotel amenities
Cabins convert from daytime sofa lounges into cozy bunk beds made with crisp linens
Iconic historic lines include the legendary Venice Simplon-Orient-Express and the transcontinental Trans-Siberian Railway
Offers multi-day scenic travel through remote landscapes with five-star gourmet culinary dining

facts_and_myths.claim: The Trans-Siberian Railway journey from Moscow to Vladivostok takes seven full days and crosses eight time zones.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Spanning 9,289 kilometers (5,772 miles), it is the longest continuous passenger rail journey on Earth.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Passengers spend a full week sleeping, eating, and drinking tea from traditional Russian glass-and-metal podstakanniks.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Orient Express was a fictional train invented by mystery novelist Agatha Christie.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Orient Express was a real luxury train running between Paris and Istanbul starting in 1883; Christie famously set a murder mystery aboard it.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Royalty, diplomats, and spies frequented the train during the height of early 20th-century espionage.

name: Auto-Rack Train
visual_anchor: Long specialized freight train composed of fully enclosed corrugated steel railcars filled with brand new factory cars.
core_traits: Specialized rail freight car designed specifically to transport new automobiles and pickup trucks from factory to distribution centers
Features bi-level or tri-level internal decks with wheel chocks to secure vehicles tightly during transit
Completely enclosed with perforated metal side screens and end doors to protect new cars from vandalism, rocks, and weather
A single tri-level autorack railcar can transport up to 15 to 18 automobiles simultaneously

facts_and_myths.claim: In early days of automobile rail shipping, new cars were shipped on open flatcars and suffered heavy theft and stone vandalism.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Open-air shipments in the 1960s resulted in stolen hubcaps, smashed windshields, and hobo vandalism, forcing railroads to invent fully enclosed autoracks.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Modern autoracks are locked tight with anti-theft security seals throughout transit.

facts_and_myths.claim: Auto-rack railcars are the shortest freight cars on the railroad.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Autoracks are among the tallest and longest freight cars in rail service, measuring 89 feet in length and over 20 feet high.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Roughly 70% of all newly manufactured vehicles in North America travel by train for at least part of their journey.

name: Ballast Tamper Train
visual_anchor: Heavy bright-yellow maintenance-of-way train vibrating hydraulic tamping tines deep into the stone track ballast under the rails.
core_traits: Specialized maintenance-of-way rail vehicle used to pack track ballast under railway tracks to make them level and durable
Uses vibrating hydraulic tines to squeeze and consolidate crushed stone ballast beneath railroad ties
Corrects track geometry alignment, curvature, and elevation using laser guidance systems
Essential for maintaining high-speed track safety and preventing derailments from uneven ground settlement

facts_and_myths.claim: Before automated tamping machines, track ballast was packed entirely by hundreds of workers with handheld picks.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Railroad track gangs had to manually shovel and pound crushed gravel beneath ties with pickaxes and tamping bars.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A modern automated tamping train can align and tamp over a mile of heavy track per hour.

facts_and_myths.claim: The crushed rocks under train tracks are just random decorative stones.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Track ballast consists of sharp, angular crushed granite engineered to interlock tightly, drain water, and absorb crushing loads.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Round river stones cannot be used because they would roll and allow the tracks to shift dangerously.

name: Aerial Tramway
visual_anchor: Panoramic glass aerial tramway cabin suspended on steel cables gliding over deep snowy mountain crevasses toward a peak.
core_traits: Aerial cable transit system where passenger cabins are suspended and propelled by overhead steel track cables
Connects valley floors with towering mountain summits, ski resorts, and across deep river gorges
Operates with two counterbalancing cars that ascend and descend in synchronized opposition
Overcomes extreme cliffs and impassable mountain terrain with zero ground track construction

facts_and_myths.claim: If the electric power cuts out, an aerial tramway cabin will plummet instantly to the ground.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The cabin is securely clamped to heavy stationary track cables; backup diesel generator engines and cable brakes safely winch cabins home.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The main steel cables have breaking strengths hundreds of times greater than the fully loaded cabin weight.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Peak 2 Peak Gondola in Whistler, Canada spans nearly two miles unsupported between towers.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It holds the world record for the longest unsupported cable span (3.03 km) suspended over 1,400 feet above the valley floor.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Some cabins feature clear glass bottoms for thrill-seeking passengers.

name: Airport People Mover
visual_anchor: Driverless modern white terminal shuttle train gliding smoothly along an elevated guideway between glass airport concourses.
core_traits: Fully automated, driverless small-scale rail or rubber-tired transit system operating on exclusive rights-of-way
Ferries airline passengers, luggage, and crew rapidly between disconnected airport terminals, concourses, and rental car hubs
Operates continuous short-loop headways (often every 2 to 3 minutes) with wide sliding doors
Controlled entirely by central supervisory computers with synchronized platform screen safety doors

facts_and_myths.claim: All airport people movers run on standard steel train tracks like conventional freight trains.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Many airport people movers use rubber tires running on smooth concrete or steel guidebeams for quieter operation and steeper climbing.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Some, like the Dallas/Fort Worth Skylink, run at 35 mph on an elevated guideway inside the airport perimeter.

facts_and_myths.claim: The world's first automated people mover system was installed at Tampa International Airport in 1971.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Designed by Westinghouse, it transferred passengers from the central landside terminal to airside gates in under a minute.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Automated people movers have virtually eliminated long, exhausting airport concourse walks for travelers.

name: Yard Switching Locomotive
visual_anchor: Compact heavy diesel switcher locomotive with low hood and all-around handrails nudging boxcars into classification yard tracks.
core_traits: Specialized small locomotive designed for assembling, sorting, and breaking up trains inside rail classification yards
Engineered for high tractive effort and low speed rather than long-distance high-speed cruising
Features low hoods and elevated cab windows to give the engineer 360-degree visibility around tight yard curves
Often operated today via remote radio belt-pack controllers by ground crew switchmen

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern yard switchers can be driven by a remote control box strapped to a ground worker's chest without anyone in the cab.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Remote Control Locomotive (RCL) systems allow a ground switchman to control throttle, brakes, and couplers while walking the tracks.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Built-in tilt sensors automatically trigger emergency brakes if the operator falls over.

facts_and_myths.claim: Switcher locomotives are lightweight engines with little pulling power.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Switchers are intentionally built with thick solid steel frame ballast plates to maximize weight and rail traction on heavy cuts of cars.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A heavy switcher can move thousands of tons of freight cars at low yard speeds.

name: Rotary Snowplow Train
visual_anchor: Mighty railway snowplow with a massive spinning circular cutting wheel blasting a towering plume of white snow across Donner Pass.
core_traits: Specialized railroad car equipped with a colossal circular rotating fan-blade cutting wheel on its front end
Cuts through massive avalanche snowdrifts and packed snowpack that would derail ordinary wedge plows
Blasts excavated snow hundreds of feet away from the tracks through an adjustable discharge chute
Pushed from behind by multiple heavy diesel locomotives over treacherous high mountain railroad passes

facts_and_myths.claim: Rotary snowplows have their own internal engines that turn the train's wheels down the track.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The internal engine solely powers the spinning cutter wheel; the entire plow car must be pushed by separate locomotives behind it.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Historically, steam rotary plows had full boilers dedicated exclusively to spinning the giant cutting wheel.

facts_and_myths.claim: Rotary snowplows can blast through snowdrifts taller than the train itself.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Equipped with folding side wings that channel snow into the 12-foot spinning rotor, they can clear drifts exceeding 20 feet deep.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Union Pacific still maintains historic operational rotary snowplows to keep the Sierra Nevada mountain tracks open.

name: Container Well Car Train
visual_anchor: Articulated three-unit well car train carrying brightly painted ocean shipping containers riding barely inches above the rails.
core_traits: Specialized railway car with a depressed center 'well' section designed to carry double-stacked intermodal shipping containers
Lowers the bottom container to ride just inches above the rail, clearing overhead bridges and tunnels
Features twistlock corner castings that lock top and bottom shipping containers securely together
Forms articulated multi-unit cars that share middle wheel bogies to reduce weight and slack action

facts_and_myths.claim: The bottom container in a well car sits higher up than on a normal flatbed train car.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The well drops down between the wheels, allowing the bottom container to sit 10 to 12 inches lower than a standard flatcar.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: This crucial foot of clearance makes double-stacking possible across thousands of miles of standard bridges.

facts_and_myths.claim: A single long double-stack container train can replace up to 300 heavy semi-trucks on the highway.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hauling hundreds of containers with just two or three crew members, intermodal well cars form the backbone of global commerce.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: They seamlessly transfer standard 40-foot and 53-foot containers between container ships and highway truck chassis.

name: Armored Train
visual_anchor: Formidable camouflaged steel-plated armored train bristling with revolving heavy artillery turrets and machine gun slits.
core_traits: Railway train protected with heavy armor plating and armed with artillery guns, autocannons, and machine gun cupolas
Widely deployed during the Russian Civil War, World War I, and World War II to secure contested rail lines and transport troops
Included armored locomotives, artillery wagons, troop-carrying infantry wagons, and anti-aircraft flatcars
Required reconnaissance 'pilot cars' pushed ahead to detonate potential track mines

facts_and_myths.claim: Leon Trotsky lived and commanded the Red Army from a famous legendary armored train during the Russian Civil War.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Trotsky's train covered thousands of miles across Russia, housing a mobile military headquarters, telegraph office, and printing press.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It even carried its own military brass band and two fighter airplanes mounted on flatcars.

facts_and_myths.claim: Armored trains were completely invulnerable to enemy infantry attacks.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Armored trains were strictly bound to fixed railway tracks; simple sabotage of a single rail or viaduct left the entire train trapped and vulnerable.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The advent of precision aerial ground-attack planes made large armored trains easy targets, leading to their decline.

name: Heritage Steam Railcar
visual_anchor: Charming polished mahogany and brass vintage self-propelled steam railcar puffing along a preserved branch line.
core_traits: Self-contained passenger railroad coach with a built-in miniature steam engine and boiler inside one end
Designed for low-cost, low-passenger branch line operations without needing a separate heavy locomotive
Popular in Victorian and Edwardian Britain and Europe before internal combustion railcars took over
Preserved today on heritage railways as operating museum treasures

facts_and_myths.claim: Steam railcars required a separate tender car coupled behind to carry water and coal.
facts_and_myths.explanation: All coal, water tanks, and the vertical firetube boiler were built into a compact engine compartment inside the coach itself.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The driver sat in a small forward glass cabin directly beside the miniature boiler.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Great Western Railway in Britain operated dozens of steam rail motors to compete with newly emerging electric street trams.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Introduced in 1903, they could stop at simple wooden roadside halts with fold-down steps, serving rural communities efficiently.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Several working examples have been meticulously restored and operate on English heritage railways today.

name: Tilting Train
visual_anchor: High-speed electric passenger train tilting gracefully inward at an angle as it powers through a sweeping track curve.
core_traits: High-speed passenger train with active hydraulic or pneumatic mechanisms that tilt the carriages into curves like a motorcycle
Compensates for lateral centrifugal forces, allowing trains to travel up to 30% faster around existing curved tracks in passenger comfort
Avoids the multi-billion dollar cost of blasting brand new straight railroad tunnels through mountains
Exemplified by the Italian Pendolino technology and the American Northeast Corridor Acela

facts_and_myths.claim: Tilting trains lean into curves to keep the train from flying off the tracks.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The tracks and wheel flanges can easily keep the train on track; the tilt exists primarily so passengers do not feel nauseous or get thrown sideways.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Early passive tilting trains actually made passengers motion-sick until modern gyro-sensors improved active tilt timing.

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern tilting trains use gyroscopes and GPS curve databases to start tilting before the car enters the turn.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Look-ahead electronic sensors calculate track geometry in advance, commanding hydraulic actuators to smoothly tilt the cars up to 8 degrees.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Amtrak's Acela uses tilting technology to run high-speed service on historic colonial-era tracks between Boston and Washington DC.

name: Electric Multiple Unit
visual_anchor: Sleek aerodynamic eight-car commuter train with rooftop pantographs pulling away from a station with rapid quiet acceleration.
core_traits: Multiple-car passenger train where electric traction motors are distributed across multiple wheel bogies throughout the train
Has no separate locomotive; all passenger coaches contribute traction and braking power
Delivers rapid, smooth acceleration and regenerative braking ideal for urban and suburban stop-and-go transit
Dominates modern passenger rail networks worldwide from suburban commuter lines to airport expresses

facts_and_myths.claim: Frank J. Sprague invented the multiple-unit traction control system in 1897.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sprague's revolutionary master-controller system allowed a single driver to control electric motors on dozens of individual cars simultaneously.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: His invention paved the way for modern subways, high-speed trains, and electric multiple units.

facts_and_myths.claim: If one motor car fails in an electric multiple unit, the entire train breaks down and cannot move.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because power is distributed across multiple cars, an EMU can simply isolate a broken motor and continue operating on remaining powered bogies.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Distributing power also prevents wheel slippage because train weight is distributed evenly across all drive wheels.

name: Mine Train
visual_anchor: Compact low-profile battery-electric mining locomotive hauling steel ore hoppers through a rugged dark rock tunnel.
core_traits: Narrow-gauge railway system operating deep inside underground mines to haul mined ore, coal, and miner crews
Features an ultra-low profile chassis designed to squeeze through tight, damp subterranean tunnels
Powered by heavy flameproof battery packs, compressed air, or overhead electric trolley wires
Engineered with explosion-proof electrical enclosures to prevent sparking in methane-rich coal mine environments

facts_and_myths.claim: Gasoline and diesel car engines were freely used in early coal mine trains without restriction.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Standard combustion engines produce lethal carbon monoxide gas and open sparks that could ignite explosive coal dust and methane pockets.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Mines used compressed air locomotives with high-pressure air tanks that exhausted cool, breathable air into the tunnels.

facts_and_myths.claim: Before mining locomotives were invented, thousands of children and pit ponies spent their entire lives hauling ore carts underground.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Small pit ponies lived permanently in underground stables, pulling heavy ore trams until electric locomotives replaced them in the 20th century.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Some British coal mines used pit ponies as late as the 1990s.

name: Rail Tanker Train
visual_anchor: Long train of cylindrical black steel pressurized tank cars rounding a curve carrying crude oil and liquid chemicals.
core_traits: Specialized cylindrical freight railcar engineered to transport liquids, petroleum, liquefied gases, and hazardous chemicals
Constructed with thick pressurized steel or aluminum cylindrical tanks with dished hemispherical ends
Equipped with pressure relief safety valves, thermal insulation blankets, and reinforced head shields to prevent punctures
Essential for moving ethanol, crude oil, liquid chlorine, and anhydrous ammonia between refineries and industrial plants

facts_and_myths.claim: Rail tank cars are simply thin steel hollow tubes with no internal safety reinforcement.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern DOT-117 tank cars feature 9/16-inch thick steel tanks, full-height 1/2-inch head shields, thermal jackets, and rollover protection.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: These strict safety upgrades were mandated after the 2013 Lac-Megantic oil train derailment in Quebec.

facts_and_myths.claim: A single rail tank car can hold up to 30,000 gallons of liquid cargo.
facts_and_myths.explanation: That is equivalent to more than three large highway semi-tanker trucks carried in a single railcar.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Some specialized tank cars feature internal heating coils to melt solidified molasses or asphalt so it can be pumped out.

name: Track Inspection Train
visual_anchor: Specialized high-speed yellow inspection train shooting laser beams and ultrasonic sound waves at the rails while speeding down the track.
core_traits: Comprehensive diagnostic laboratory train that tests and inspects railroad tracks for microscopic cracks and rail wear
Uses ultrasonic testing and electromagnetic induction to detect hidden internal steel fractures inside the rail heads
Equipped with laser profilometers, optical cameras, and accelerometers to measure track gauge, alignment, and overhead catenary wire wear
Japan's famous high-speed Shinkansen test train is celebrated as 'Doctor Yellow' by train enthusiasts

facts_and_myths.claim: Spotting the bright yellow 'Doctor Yellow' test train in Japan is widely believed to bring good luck.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because its inspection schedules are secret and not published to the public, seeing it streak by is considered a rare lucky omen.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It tests the entire Shinkansen high-speed rail line at full 270 km/h operational speeds.

facts_and_myths.claim: Ultrasonic track testing was invented only in the 21st century.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Dr. Elmer Sperry built the first practical induction rail flaw detector car back in 1928, saving countless trains from derailments.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Modern inspection cars can scan rails at over 60 mph while pinpointing flaws the size of a pinhead.

name: Hybrid Passenger Train
visual_anchor: Modern aerodynamic regional train seamlessly retracting its roof pantograph as it transitions from electrified line to battery power.
core_traits: Passenger train capable of operating from overhead electric catenary lines and switching to onboard batteries or hydrogen fuel cells
Enables continuous one-seat passenger journeys across electrified mainline tracks and non-electrified rural branch lines
Features lithium-titanate battery packs that recharge while cruising under overhead electric wires or via regenerative braking
Eliminates diesel exhaust emissions on non-electrified regional railway corridors

facts_and_myths.claim: Germany introduced the world's first fleet of 100% hydrogen-powered passenger trains in commercial service.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Alstom Coradia iLint uses hydrogen fuel cells to combine hydrogen with oxygen, producing pure electricity and emitting only steam water.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It can travel 1,000 kilometers on a single tank of hydrogen at speeds up to 140 km/h.

facts_and_myths.claim: Battery trains can only travel 5 miles before needing an 8-hour charge.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern battery-electric multiple units achieve operational ranges exceeding 50 to 80 miles on pure battery power.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: They can fast-charge at terminus stations in just 15 minutes while passengers board.

name: Funicular Railway
visual_anchor: Stepped glass-roofed funicular car climbing a sheer green cliff face connecting a seaside harbor with the mountain town above.
core_traits: Steep incline railway system with two passenger counterbalanced cars permanently attached to opposite ends of a single haulage cable
As one car ascends the mountain slope, the other descends, with their weights naturally counterbalancing each other
Features tiered interior compartments and angled floors so passengers stand and sit level on steep hills
Passes each other halfway up the slope at a central automated Abt passing loop

facts_and_myths.claim: Because the two cars counterbalance each other, funiculars require very little electrical energy to operate.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The descending car's gravitational pull does most of the heavy lifting to pull the ascending car up, requiring only a modest electric motor.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Some historic funiculars used water ballast tanks: the car at the top filled with water to become heavier and pull the bottom car up!

facts_and_myths.claim: Funicular railways and street cable cars are the exact same mechanical system.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A funicular has two linked cars counterbalancing on one closed cable; a street cable car clamps and unclamps from a continuous loop cable.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Stoos Funicular in Switzerland is the world's steepest, climbing a mind-boggling 110% gradient (47.7 degrees).

name: Vintage Trolley
visual_anchor: Historic cream-and-burgundy streamline PCC trolley clanging its brass foot bell along a leafy brick-paved historic street.
core_traits: Classic electric street railway car of the early-to-mid 20th century drawing power via an arched rooftop trolley pole
Iconic models include the streamlined Presidents' Conference Committee (PCC) car with rounded art-deco styling
Fitted with foot-pedal acceleration and braking controls that inspired automotive driver ergonomics
Features polished wooden slatted bench seats, incandescent globe interior lights, and brass pull cords for stop requests

facts_and_myths.claim: The PCC streetcar was designed in the 1930s by a committee of transit company presidents to save the streetcar industry.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Facing fierce competition from private automobiles, the committee spent millions standardizing a quiet, fast, streamlined streetcar.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: PCC cars were so smooth and responsive that thousands were built and operated in cities across North America and Europe.

facts_and_myths.claim: Trolley cars were called 'trolleys' because passengers pushed them like grocery carts.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The name came from the small wheeled current collector pulley called a 'troller' that was pulled along overhead electric wires.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Brooklyn Dodgers baseball team was named after pedestrians who had to 'dodge' the speeding electric trolleys of Brooklyn.

name: Sailboat
visual_anchor: Graceful white monohull sailboat heeling into azure Caribbean swells with billowing triangular sails catching fresh wind.
core_traits: Watercraft propelled primarily or partly by sails harnessing natural wind power across canvas or Dacron
Features a deep ballast keel or retractable centerboard to prevent drifting sideways in the water
Steered using a stern rudder connected to a steering wheel or wooden tiller arm
One of humanity's oldest long-distance exploration tools, circumnavigating the globe for centuries

facts_and_myths.claim: Sailboats can only travel in the exact same direction that the wind is blowing.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern sails act as vertical airplane wings, generating aerodynamic lift that allows boats to sail upwind at sharp 45-degree angles.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: By zig-zagging back and forth (tacking), a sailboat can sail directly toward the origin of the wind.

facts_and_myths.claim: High-tech America's Cup racing sailboats can sail three to four times faster than the actual speed of the wind.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Foiling sailboats generate their own apparent wind, lifting completely out of the water on hydrofoils to exceed 50 knots in 15-knot breezes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Carbon-fiber hydrofoils reduce water friction to near zero.

name: Luxury Yacht
visual_anchor: Gleaming multi-deck 300-foot white superyacht anchored in Monaco harbor at twilight with illuminated underwater blue lights.
core_traits: Large, privately owned recreational motor or sailing vessel equipped with luxury living quarters and amenities
Often exceeds 100 to 300 feet in length, featuring helipads, infinity pools, beach clubs, and submarine garages
Powered by heavy marine diesel engines coupled to waterjet drives or twin screw propellers
Maintained by full-time professional crews including captains, engineers, deckhands, and private chefs

facts_and_myths.claim: The world's largest private superyacht, Azzam, is longer than many commercial cruise ships.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Measuring 590 feet (180 meters) in length, Azzam features over 94,000 horsepower and cruises at over 30 knots.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It holds an armored master suite, missile defense systems, and a private submarine.

facts_and_myths.claim: Yachts do not need to register with any country or follow international maritime laws.
facts_and_myths.explanation: All yachts must be flagged with a recognized national maritime registry and obey the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many superyachts are flagged in the Cayman Islands, Bermuda, or Marshall Islands.

name: Cruise Ship
visual_anchor: Colossal eighteen-deck passenger cruise liner gliding into a tropical port with waterslides, theater domes, and thousands of balcony staterooms.
core_traits: Massive passenger ocean vessel designed for vacation voyages where the voyage experience itself is the primary attraction
Accommodates 3,000 to 7,000 passengers with multi-story restaurants, theaters, swimming pools, and casino decks
Powered by massive diesel-electric powerplants driving rotatable underwater azimuth thruster pods (Azipods)
Features dynamic computer-controlled gyroscopic fin stabilizers to minimize ship rolling in rough seas

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern cruise ships have deep V-shaped hulls that reach hundreds of feet down into the ocean to avoid tipping over.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern cruise ships have surprisingly shallow drafts (about 30 feet) with wide, flat-bottomed hull geometry to access shallow Caribbean ports.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The ship's stability comes from its enormous beam width and computerized water ballast trimming systems.

facts_and_myths.claim: The largest modern cruise ships are more than five times larger by gross tonnage than the historic RMS Titanic.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Royal Caribbean's Icon of the Seas exceeds 250,000 gross tons, compared to the Titanic's 46,000 gross tons.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It can produce over 2 million liters of fresh drinking water daily from seawater via reverse osmosis desalination.

name: Container Ship
visual_anchor: Gigantic 400-meter container ship stacked ten stories high with thousands of colorful steel containers transiting the Suez Canal.
core_traits: Cargo vessel specialized to transport intermodal freight containers across global ocean shipping routes
Constructed with cell guides inside the hull that allow standard 20-foot and 40-foot containers to slot securely in place
Powered by colossal two-stroke turbocharged low-speed marine diesel engines standing four stories tall
Forms the absolute lifeblood of modern economic globalization, carrying 90% of manufactured world goods

facts_and_myths.claim: Malcom McLean invented the intermodal container shipping system in 1956, revolutionizing world trade.
facts_and_myths.explanation: McLean realized packing standard steel boxes directly from truck to ship slashed port loading times from days to hours.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Standardization reduced the cost of loading cargo by over 90% almost overnight.

facts_and_myths.claim: The largest modern container ships require over 100 sailors to crew the ship across oceans.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Due to immense bridge automation and computerized engine monitoring, a 400-meter ship carrying 24,000 containers operates with just 20 to 25 crew members.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The main engine propeller shaft on a mega container ship is nearly two feet in diameter of solid forged steel.

name: Cargo Ship
visual_anchor: Heavy ocean freighter plowing through choppy gray waters with deck cranes positioned over vast open hold hatches.
core_traits: Merchant vessel designed to transport non-containerized dry bulk goods, raw commodities, and break-bulk machinery
Features cavernous internal cargo holds designed to carry grain, iron ore, bauxite, coal, and timber
Often equipped with onboard rotating deck cranes and clamshell grabs to load and unload at unequipped ports
Operates across all international sea lanes under strict global maritime trade conventions

facts_and_myths.claim: Bulk cargo ships carrying dry grain must be loaded tightly to prevent the cargo from shifting and flipping the ship.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Dry grain acts like a liquid; if a hold is half empty, grain slides to one side during rough waves, causing catastrophic vessel capsizing.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: International maritime regulations require specialized shifting boards and grain trimming to prevent grain movement.

facts_and_myths.claim: Cargo ships travel faster than modern passenger airliners across the ocean.
facts_and_myths.explanation: To maximize fuel economy, bulk freighters cruise at slow economic speeds of roughly 12 to 16 knots (14 to 18 mph).
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Slow steaming cuts ship fuel consumption and carbon emissions by up to 30%.

name: Oil Tanker
visual_anchor: Massive red-hulled ultra-large crude carrier sitting low in the water laden with millions of barrels of crude oil.
core_traits: Specialized merchant vessel designed for the bulk transportation of crude oil and refined petroleum products
Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCC) exceed 1,000 feet in length and carry over 2 million barrels of crude oil
Constructed with mandatory double hulls featuring an outer and inner steel skin separated by ballast void spaces
Features extensive deck piping networks, inert gas explosion prevention systems, and high-capacity cargo pumps

facts_and_myths.claim: The Seawise Giant was the longest and heaviest ship ever constructed in human history.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Measuring 1,504 feet (458 meters) long and fully loaded at 657,000 tonnes displacement, it was longer than the Empire State Building is tall.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It was so massive that it could not navigate the English Channel, Suez Canal, or Panama Canal.

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern oil tankers can still be built with a single steel hull bottom.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Following the 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill, international maritime law strictly mandated double hulls for all oil tankers worldwide.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A double hull provides a 2-meter protective safety buffer that prevents oil spills if the outer hull is punctured.

name: Aircraft Carrier
visual_anchor: Nuclear supercarrier plowing through the Pacific with an angled flight deck launching a supersonic fighter jet via electromagnetic catapult.
core_traits: Colossal warship designed as a mobile seagoing airbase featuring a full-length flight deck and hangar bay
Powered by nuclear reactors allowing decades of continuous high-speed cruising without refueling
Launches combat fighter jets using steam or Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS) catapults
Recovers returning landing jets using heavy-duty arresting steel wires caught by the aircraft's tailhook

facts_and_myths.claim: US Navy nuclear aircraft carriers carry enough nuclear reactor fuel to operate continuously for over 20 years without refueling.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Enriched uranium reactor cores provide unlimited global range and generate electrical power comparable to a city of 100,000 people.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The ship's desalination plants generate 400,000 gallons of fresh water every day.

facts_and_myths.claim: Fighter jets land on aircraft carriers by rolling to a gentle, gradual stop using wheel brakes like normal airports.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Jets hit the deck at 150 mph with engines at full military power; an arresting steel cable snags the tailhook, slamming the plane to zero in 2 seconds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pilots apply full thrust on touchdown so they can immediately take off again if the tailhook misses the wires.

name: Battleship
visual_anchor: Heavily armored Iowa-class battleship firing a devastating full nine-gun broadside of 16-inch artillery pushing massive ocean shockwaves.
core_traits: Massive heavily armored capital warship armed with gigantic main-battery naval artillery guns
Pioneered in 1906 by Britain's revolutionary all-big-gun HMS Dreadnought
Protected by thick forged steel armor belts up to 12 to 16 inches thick over vital magazines and engine rooms
Served as the supreme symbol of naval supremacy until naval aviation and guided missiles eclipsed gun warfare

facts_and_myths.claim: The Yamato and Musashi of the Imperial Japanese Navy were the heaviest and most powerfully armed battleships in history.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Displacing over 72,000 tons loaded, they carried nine gargantuan 18.1-inch (460 mm) guns that fired 3,200-pound shells over 26 miles.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Each gun turret weighed more than an entire average naval destroyer.

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern world navies still actively build brand new battleships today.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Battleships became obsolete after World War II as aircraft carriers and guided missile destroyers could strike targets hundreds of miles further away.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: All surviving iconic battleships, like the USS Missouri and USS Iowa, now serve as floating historic museum ships.

name: Naval Destroyer
visual_anchor: Stealth-profile guided missile destroyer cutting through heavy ocean spray with phased-array Aegis radar arrays scanning the horizon.
core_traits: Fast, highly maneuverable multi-mission warship designed to defend fleets against aircraft, submarines, and anti-ship missiles
Equipped with Aegis combat weapon systems, SPY phased-array radar, and Vertical Launch Systems (VLS)
Carries a diverse arsenal of Tomahawk cruise missiles, anti-aircraft interceptors, and anti-submarine torpedoes
Operates advanced sonar domes in its bow and deploys embarked MH-60 Seahawk helicopters for submarine hunting

facts_and_myths.claim: Destroyers were originally invented in the late 1800s specifically to destroy small enemy torpedo boats.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Originally called 'torpedo boat destroyers', they evolved from small fast gunboats into the versatile backbone of modern navies.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Modern destroyers are larger and heavier than many World War II light cruisers.

facts_and_myths.claim: Destroyers rely primarily on visual lookout binoculars to detect incoming supersonic anti-ship missiles.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Destroyers use automated Aegis phased-array radar systems that automatically track hundreds of airborne targets and launch interceptors in split seconds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Close-In Weapon Systems (CIWS) like Phalanx can fire 4,500 armor-piercing tungsten rounds per minute at incoming missiles.

name: Speedboat
visual_anchor: Sleek aerodynamic offshore racing powerboat flying across turquoise waves with twin rooster tails of white water spray arching high.
core_traits: Small, high-speed motorboat powered by one or more powerful outboard or inboard marine gasoline engines
Features a planing hull design that rises out of the water at high speed to reduce hydrodynamic drag
Used extensively for recreational watersports, water skiing, wakeboarding, and offshore powerboat racing
Steered via an automotive-style steering wheel and marine throttle lever

facts_and_myths.claim: Speedboats push through water like a heavy barge no matter how fast they travel.
facts_and_myths.explanation: At high speed, speedboats 'plane', skimming on top of the surface water to reduce friction by over 80%.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The hydrodynamics of a planing hull allows dramatic acceleration and tight carving turns.

facts_and_myths.claim: Ken Warby set the world water speed record in a backyard-built jet speedboat at 317.6 mph (511 km/h).
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 1978, Australian Ken Warby built 'Spirit of Australia' out of wood and a surplus jet engine, setting a record that stands to this day.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Water speed record attempts are among the most dangerous motor sports on Earth, with an 85% fatality rate among record contenders.

name: Jet Ski
visual_anchor: Agile personal watercraft carving hard through a wave crest sending a sheet of glittering spray into the tropical sunshine.
core_traits: Recreational watercraft that the rider sits or stands on, rather than sitting inside a traditional cockpit
Propelled by an internal waterjet impeller pump that sucks water from under the hull and shoots a high-pressure jet out the stern
Has zero exposed propeller blades, dramatically reducing danger to swimmers and marine wildlife
Steered by turning the direction of the waterjet nozzle via handlebar grips

facts_and_myths.claim: If you completely let go of the throttle on an older Jet Ski, you can still steer away from an obstacle.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because steering relies entirely on directional waterjet thrust, cutting the throttle off completely eliminates steering control.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Modern PWCs include off-throttle assisted steering computers to prevent collisions.

facts_and_myths.claim: Clayton Jacobson II invented the personal watercraft in the 1960s after being injured in a motorcycle accident.
facts_and_myths.explanation: He wanted to enjoy motorcycle-style thrill riding on forgiving water instead of dangerous asphalt pavement.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Kawasaki licensed his design to launch the famous stand-up 'Jet Ski' brand in 1973.

name: Canoe
visual_anchor: Classic wooden cedar-strip open canoe gliding silently across a glassy forest lake surrounded by autumn reflections.
core_traits: Lightweight narrow watercraft with pointed ends and an open top, propelled using single-bladed paddles
